WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) today announced the financial close of a loan of up to $1.9 billion to NextEra Energy to help finance the restart of the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Linn County, Iowa. The investment will bring Iowa's only nuclear power plant back online, advancing President Trump's energy dominance agenda and Executive Order, Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base.

“President Trump has set an ambitious course to restore American nuclear leadership, and the restart of Duane Arnold Nuclear Plant in Iowa marks another step in advancing America’s nuclear renaissance,” said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly. “Returning 615 megawatts of reliable baseload generation will drive down electricity costs, while supporting thousands of American jobs. This Administration is pursuing a comprehensive nuclear strategy, restarting existing reactors, increasing the output of our nuclear fleet, and accelerating new construction, to build the abundant, affordable, and reliable power system required for American prosperity and reindustrialization.”

Duane Arnold’s restart will add 615 megawatts (MW) of reliable baseload power back on the grid—enough to power nearly 500,000 homes—and help meet growing electricity demand in Iowa and across the region. The project will create nearly 1,500 American jobs during construction and support more than 450 jobs during operations.

It is a pleasure to be present with you today. Throughout my professional journey, I have had the opportunity to engage with issues that impact rural communities, particularly in relation to access to financial resources. My experiences at the Federal Reserve have further enhanced my understanding of both the opportunities and challenges faced by rural America, particularly as I have traveled extensively to various rural areas over the past several years.

Notably, these communities tend to encounter numerous difficulties, and they may also face unique obstacles that require adaptable solutions. What has particularly resonated with me is the degree of innovation and creativity that can often be observed in many of these solutions. It appears that we should actively seek to highlight these examples, disseminating successful practices and promoting ideas that may help expand opportunities and bolster economic growth throughout rural America.

For instance, in 2023, I had the chance to journey along the Blues Trail in the Mississippi Delta, traversing the route from Jackson to Memphis. Along this path, I engaged with local leaders and representatives from financial institutions, some of whom are here today, to gain insights into how once-thriving rural railroad towns are adjusting to both enduring and emerging challenges.

In Moorhead, Mississippi, which is often recognized as the location where the Southern crosses the Yellow Dog, I observed how a bank that had faced difficulties in maintaining its branch ultimately decided to donate its building to a community development financial institution, thereby preserving crucial access to banking services for a community that greatly requires this support.

Furthermore, in Clarksdale, Mississippi, I had the opportunity to visit the Travelers Hotel, which underwent redevelopment through the utilization of New Markets Tax Credits. This project now plays a significant role in the revitalization of the Blues tourism sector within that historic community. Overall, these experiences illustrate the importance of innovative approaches in addressing the challenges faced by rural communities.

It is worth noting that at the time of the previous framework review during 2019 and 2020, policymakers were considering an economy that had for many years demonstrated low growth, low inflation, and a very flat Phillips curve, which means that inflation was not very responsive to slack in the economy. Moreover, the overarching concern for central bankers at that time was how to operate when short-term interest rates are near the effective lower bound. The changes implemented as a result of this review were a logical progression, not a change in course, grounded in our ever-evolving understanding of our economy. I will make note of four adjustments to the consensus statement and discuss each in turn.

First, the revised consensus statement removed language emphasizing the effective lower bound (ELB) as a defining feature of the economic landscape. Instead, it states that our monetary policy strategy is designed to promote maximum employment and stable prices across a broad range of economic conditions. This revision, reflecting a move away from the post–financial crisis era of historically low interest rates, makes our framework more robust. It is useful to recall that at the time of the FOMC's previous framework review, during 2019 and 2020, policymakers were considering an economy that had for many years demonstrated low growth, low inflation, and a very flat Phillips curve—meaning that inflation was not very responsive to slack in the economy. The overarching concern for central bankers at that time was how to operate when short-term interest rates are near the ELB. Today, of course, we are operating in a very different environment, at least in part brought on by the economic consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic.

input: In the present day, the Federal Reserve tends to communicate through a variety of channels, and these can often include speeches by policymakers, press conferences held by Chair Powell, and even the Fed's social media outlets. It is worth noting that clear and ample communication has not always appeared to be a hallmark of the Fed, and this may reflect a gradual shift in institutional practice. Additionally, in the 1990s, cable news outlets would often attempt to spot former Fed Chair Alan Greenspan as he walked into the building on the day of FOMC meetings. Furthermore, commentators would pay careful attention to the size of his briefcase, and the thought was that a bulging briefcase would suggest the Chair was advocating a rate change with documents to convince fellow policymakers. In essence, a light bag, on the contrary, would have signaled that a status quo policy decision was likely, and this interpretation appears to have shaped media coverage at the time. Notably, former Chair Greenspan seemed to value the element of surprise, and in 1987 he famously quipped that if he seemed unduly clear to his audience, they must have misunderstood what he said. That said, during his tenure in later years, he initiated substantial changes in how Fed policymakers communicate with the public, and this can often be seen as a move toward greater transparency. Ultimately, the Fed's communication approach has experienced a gradual evolution from ambiguity toward clearer public engagement.

It is worth noting that community banks ought to be subject to rigorous supervisory oversight; however, this oversight must correspond to their relatively smaller size, less complex business activities, and the limited risks they may pose to the financial stability of the United States. Furthermore, this objective can be achieved by establishing a distinct oversight program for community banks that is separate from those intended for larger and regional financial institutions, thereby allowing examiners to concentrate specifically on the risks and activities pertinent to small banks. This approach would also diminish the inclination to apply standards and expectations originally designed for larger, more complex institutions to community banks.

This identification does not suggest an exclusive focus on merely checking compliance boxes while reviewing processes, procedures, and documentation, irrespective of the actual assessment of risk. Moreover, it does not imply neglecting other critical components of the established supervisory program.

As noted in the supervisory operating principles, an emphasis on material financial risks necessitates that examiners employ reasoned judgment in prioritizing issues throughout each phase of the examination process. This prioritization commences with the focus outlined in the pre-examination letter, continues through the scope of work during the examination, and involves distinguishing between findings that warrant formal attention and those that may be resolved through less formal avenues. The operating principles explicitly mention supervisory observations for matters that do not constitute violations but may still be documented in the examination report. Ultimately, this approach seeks to enhance the effectiveness of the supervisory process while ensuring that community banks are evaluated in a manner that is appropriate for their specific context.
output:
Community banks should be subject to strict supervisory oversight, but it must be commensurate with their smaller size, simpler business activities, and the modest risks they pose to U.S. financial stability. This could be accomplished by separating the community bank oversight program from those designed for larger and regional banks, focusing examiner attention on small bank risks and activities. This would also eliminate the temptation to "push down" standards and expectations to community banks, that were designed for larger and more complex institutions.

Material Financial Risk To avoid confusion, it may also be helpful to clarify what is meant by identifying material financial risks in the supervisory process. It does not mean focusing primarily on checking boxes in reviewing processes, procedures, and documentation, regardless of the assessment of risk. It also does not mean ignoring other aspects of the established supervisory program.

As the supervisory operating principles note, focusing on material financial risks requires examiners to use reasoned judgment to prioritize through every stage of an examination. This begins with targeting in the pre-examination letter, the examination's scope of work, and differentiating between findings that meet the threshold of a matter requiring attention, and those that can be addressed through less formal means. Additionally, it is important to note that prices remain considerably higher than they were prior to the pandemic, which continues to exert a negative influence on consumer sentiment. Higher prices disproportionately affect lower- and moderate-income households, as these households allocate a significantly greater proportion of their income to essential categories such as food, energy, and housing. Moreover, the price increases in these categories have significantly outpaced the general rate of inflation over the past few years.

Moreover, economic growth has moderated in the earlier part of this year, following stronger performance the previous year. It is notable that private domestic final purchases (PDFP) growth has remained robust, demonstrating a slower decline compared to gross domestic product (GDP), as the slowdown in GDP growth was partially attributable to volatile categories, including net exports, which suggests that the underlying economic growth is stronger than what the GDP figures indicate. Furthermore, PDFP has continued to show solid growth thus far in the third quarter, despite some additional weakening in housing activity, as retail sales have demonstrated further substantial gains during the months of July and August. In summary, while there are indications of progress in addressing inflation and sustaining economic growth, significant challenges remain that warrant continued attention.
output:

Private domestic final purchases (PDFP) growth has been solid and slowed much less than gross domestic product (GDP), as the slowdown in GDP growth was partly driven by volatile categories including net exports, suggesting that underlying economic growth was stronger than GDP indicated. PDFP has continued to increase at a solid pace so far in the third quarter, despite some further weakening in housing activity, as retail sales have shown further robust gains in July and August.

In the context of overseeing holding companies, it is important to note that the Federal Reserve is mandated by statute to depend "to the fullest extent possible" on the examinations conducted by the primary state or federal supervisors of subsidiary banks. In practice, this requirement can often impose considerable limitations on the supervisory activities of the Federal Reserve. This situation tends to apply to national banks that are regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) as well as state non-member banks that fall under the purview of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and a state banking authority.

This statutory requirement is intended to minimize the potential for redundant and burdensome examination processes. Nevertheless, it is essential for the Federal Reserve to possess confidence in the supervisory processes and outcomes of the examinations conducted by the OCC, FDIC, and state banking agencies. Achieving this confidence typically necessitates access to and a comprehensive review of examination reports and related activities. In situations where reliance on such examinations is not feasible or where access to supporting documentation is unavailable, it may be necessary for the Federal Reserve to initiate its own review.

Furthermore, each bank examination culminates in the creation of a report of examination, which serves to document the findings of the examination. This report frequently includes supervisory observations or criticisms, as well as matters requiring attention (MRAs) or matters requiring immediate attention (MRIAs) when such issues are identified during the examination process. Additionally, the report contains the bank's supervisory ratings, which are determined according to the CAMELS rating system.

It is worth noting that the findings from examinations and the inclusion of specific matters within the report can have significant implications for the bank involved. Not only do they guide how banks prioritize their efforts to address identified issues, but the bank's CAMELS rating can also influence its eligibility for favorable treatment regarding banking applications, impact the cost of FDIC insurance premiums, affect the liquidity funding costs, and serve as an indicator of bank management performance for its board of directors. In conclusion, the intricate relationship between examination findings and their consequences highlights the importance of thorough oversight in maintaining the health of financial institutions.
output:
Reducing Overlap in Examinations In conducting holding company supervision, the Federal Reserve is required by statute to rely "to the fullest extent possible" on examinations performed by a subsidiary bank's primary state or federal supervisors. In practice, complying with this requirement imposes significant limits on the Fed's supervisory activities. This applies to national banks regulated by the OCC and state non-member banks regulated by the FDIC and a state banking regulator.

The requirement is designed to avoid redundant and burdensome examination processes. However, to be effective, the Fed must have confidence in the supervisory processes and outcomes of these OCC, FDIC, and state banking agency exams, which requires access to and a thorough review of examination reports and activities. Where it is not possible to rely on or we do not have access to an exam or supporting documentation of supervisory activity, we may need to conduct our own review.

Reports of Examination and Supervisory Ratings Each bank examination concludes with a report of examination. This report documents exam findings including any supervisory observations or criticisms, and matters requiring attention (MRAs) or matters requiring immediate attention (MRIAs), if any are found during the exam. The report also includes the bank's supervisory ratings according to the CAMELS rating system.

Exam findings and the inclusion of specific matters in the report can have serious consequences for the bank. In addition to directing how banks prioritize their efforts to remediate identified issues, the bank's CAMELS rating can influence whether the bank qualifies to receive favorable treatment of banking applications, affect the cost of FDIC insurance premiums, affect the cost of liquidity funding, and serve as an indication of bank management performance for its board of directors.

When the costs associated with running a bank increase, there tends to be a necessity for making adjustments if the institution hopes to sustain its profitability and, ultimately, its continued operation. This situation may often involve either reducing expenses or increasing fees for banking services.

Furthermore, it is worth considering how the realities of managing a business can inform our current regulatory approaches. This question becomes particularly significant when regulators contemplate the introduction of new or revised rules. Regulators may benefit from consistently evaluating three key areas: first, identifying the specific problem that the new regulation seeks to address; second, assessing the potential costs associated with this regulatory approach; and third, exploring alternative methods that might be available. Before delving into the proposed path forward, it is useful to present an example that illustrates this important concern.

Notably, the final regulations under the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) released in 2023 established new thresholds that categorize banks as "small," "intermediate," or "large." In this context, large banks are defined as those possessing more than $2 billion in assets. It appears that this rulemaking may have represented a missed opportunity to better align the CRA requirements with the realities faced by community banks, as it does not seem to recognize the fundamental distinctions among banks that operate with various balance sheets and business models. In essence, applying the same evaluation criteria to a bank with $2 billion in assets as to a bank with $2 trillion in assets may reflect an oversight regarding the essential differences among financial institutions, as well as the disproportionate costs that these regulations may impose on smaller banks.
output:
When a bank's costs increase, there is, by necessity, a need to make changes if the bank hopes to maintain profitability and ultimately its survival. This usually involves either cutting costs or raising prices on banking services.

How do the realities of operating a business inform our current approach to regulation? The question becomes acutely relevant when regulators consider imposing new or revised regulations. Furthermore, an illustrative example arises when the rate of inflation is at or below the intended target, while employment levels appear to be near or exceeding estimates of their maximum potential. It is worth noting that, as articulated in the consensus statement of the Federal Open Market Committee, the concept of maximum employment lacks a direct means of measurement and tends to evolve over time, primarily due to factors that are largely non-monetary in nature. Additionally, alterations in the economic structure that are anticipated to persist in the long term may lead to employment levels rising above current assessments of maximum employment, without necessarily exerting upward pressure on inflation beyond the benchmark of 2 percent. The coexistence of low inflation and low unemployment may often signify the presence of favorable supply shocks that are gradually influencing the economy. In such circumstances, in the absence of risks to price stability, the dual mandate objectives may not inherently conflict, and employment levels that appear to exceed their estimated maximum may not necessitate an immediate policy response. This particular dynamic was evident during the latter half of the 1990s, when then-Chairman Alan Greenspan directed the Federal Open Market Committee to refrain from raising interest rates, despite unemployment rates falling below the estimated natural levels, as robust productivity growth facilitated a scenario characterized by both strong output growth and low, decreasing inflation.

In conclusion, it may be beneficial to consider an instance that illustrates the potential tension between our overarching goals, wherein inflation levels are somewhat elevated, the labor market appears weak or is experiencing a decline, and the policy stance has already adopted an accommodative nature. Under such conditions, the need to balance the objectives of maximizing employment and ensuring price stability would suggest maintaining the policy rate at an accommodative level.
output:
Another example is when inflation is at or below target but employment seems near or higher than estimates of its maximum level and the policy stance is close to neutral or accommodative. As described in the FOMC's consensus statement, maximum employment is not directly measurable and evolves over time due to factors that are largely non-monetary. Changes to the underlying structure of the economy that are expected to persist in the longer run may result in employment rising above existing assessments of maximum employment without necessarily generating upward pressure on inflation above 2 percent. The combination of low inflation and low unemployment may reflect positive supply shocks that are working their way through the economy. In that case, absent price-stability risks, the dual-mandate objectives may not necessarily be in tension, and employment that appears stronger than its estimated maximum level may not require a policy response. This dynamic occurred during the second half of the 1990s, when then-Chairman Greenspan led the FOMC to hold off on rate increases even as unemployment moved below the estimated natural rates, as strong productivity growth allowed for a combination of strong output growth and low and falling inflation.

I will conclude this part of the discussion with an example of tension between our goals, with inflation somewhat elevated, a weak or weakening labor market, and a policy stance that is already accommodative. Under these conditions, balancing the maximum-employment and price-stability goals would call for holding the policy rate at an accommodative level.

output:

It is worth noting that the regulators entrusted with the implementation of regulations, supervision, and guidance hold the ultimate responsibility for the decisions related to policy choices. Additionally, this process can often greatly benefit from increased interaction between federal regulators and their counterparts in state bank regulation. By fostering more extensive dialogue with state regulators, it may be possible to enhance proposals during the formulation stage through the sharing of practical, real-world perspectives, which include valuable observations regarding both intended and unintended consequences of reforms. While anticipating unintended consequences presents significant challenges, casting a wide net for diverse viewpoints may lead to more effective, less disruptive, and better-informed policy decisions.

Furthermore, the importance of strengthening coordination between state regulators and the Federal Reserve is paramount. At a recent meeting of the Board's Subcommittee on Smaller Regional and Community Banking, my colleagues and I had the distinct pleasure of welcoming representatives from the Conference of State Bank Supervisors, which included four members of their State Bank Commissioner cohort. During this meeting, we gained first-hand insights into the successes, frustrations, concerns, and potential areas for improvement in the collaboration between state and federal regulators. Such direct conversations are invaluable, as they contribute significantly to building and enhancing these essential intergovernmental relationships.

Moreover, historically, one of the many commendable attributes of the Federal Reserve Board is its structural incentive to collaborate in order to achieve compromise. The governors operate under extended, staggered terms designed to shield them from the immediate influences of political considerations. The Board is composed of seven independent governors who frequently contribute their distinct perspectives on a variety of policy issues. While instances of dissent may attract considerable attention, the Federal Reserve has a long-standing tradition of engaging in thoughtful debates, exchanging views, and ultimately reaching more sustainable compromises on matters of rulemaking. The prevailing consensus on bank regulatory issues is not unexpected, as we work collectively toward the shared objectives of safety, soundness, and financial stability.

I did not envision that I would eventually become a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors or even pursue a career as an economist, as I initially entered Spelman College as a major in physics and philosophy. It was only several years post-graduation, following an unanticipated encounter, that I began to view economics as a viable avenue for my career aspirations. At that particular time, I was furthering my studies in philosophy while residing in Senegal, and I encountered challenges in identifying the appropriate framework through which to investigate the significant questions that inspired and motivated me. Consequently, I made the decision to embark on an adventurous journey: hiking Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania. Fortuitously, during this expedition, I encountered a British economist who, by the conclusion of my trek, persuaded me that economics possesses the necessary tools to engage with the questions I held in high regard. Within a few months, I returned to my home, enrolled in classes to prepare for a Ph.D. in economics, and commenced a trajectory that eventually led me to both Michigan State University and the Federal Reserve.

Today, as you prepare to leave the familiar environment of Case Hall and East Lansing, ready to embark on your next adventure, it is worth noting that I would like to present four guiding principles for you to consider as you navigate the journey that lies ahead: hope, curiosity, persistence, and a steadfast commitment to the principles of public service.
output:
When I was in your shoes, graduating from Spelman College, I remember feeling unsure of what the world would have in store for me. I did not imagine I would be a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, or even an economist. (I started Spelman as a physics and philosophy major.) I only came to see economics as a potential route several years after my graduation, following a chance encounter. At the time, I was continuing my studies in philosophy in Senegal and was struggling to find the right prism through which to explore big questions that interested and motivated me. I decided to set out for an adventure of a lifetime: hike Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania. As luck would have it, during that journey I met a British economist. By the end of the trek, he convinced me that economics held the tools to address the questions I cared about deeply. Within months, I moved back home, enrolled in classes to prepare for a Ph.D. in economics, and began a path that ultimately led me to both Michigan State and the Federal Reserve.

Today, you are leaving the safe harbor of Case Hall and East Lansing, ready to depart on your next adventure. As you do, I would like to offer four guides for you to navigate your journey ahead: hope, curiosity, persistence, and a commitment to public service.

It is worth noting that I expressed support for the Federal Open Market Committee's decision to maintain interest rates at our most recent policy meeting in March. Additionally, while economic growth has remained robust, there are early indications that it may be experiencing a slowdown. Labor market conditions have remained stable through February, and progress regarding inflation has eased; however, the overall outlook appears to be uncertain. These circumstances led me to advocate for maintaining the policy rate at what I consider a moderately restrictive level.

Furthermore, the long-term perspective illustrated by figure 9 indicates that the Federal Open Market Committee responded to the elevated inflationary environment following the pandemic by increasing the policy rate by 5.25 percentage points over a span of approximately 15 months, beginning in March 2022. After maintaining the rate at this restrictive level for more than a year, improvements in inflation allowed a reduction of the policy rate by a full percentage point last year, resulting in the current rate. The experience of inflation moderating toward the 2 percent target without a significant rise in unemployment has been historically unusual, but it is greatly welcomed.

In considering the future trajectory of policy, I intend to continuously evaluate incoming data, the developing economic outlook, and the balance of associated risks. Ultimately, it is important to emphasize that monetary policy does not follow a predetermined path. If economic conditions remain strong and inflation does not progress sustainably toward 2 percent, the present policy restraint may need to be preserved for an extended period. Conversely, should the labor market weaken unexpectedly or inflation decline more rapidly than anticipated, adjustments to policy may be warranted. In my assessment, there is no immediate necessity to expedite further changes to the policy rate. The current policy stance appears to be well positioned to address the risks and uncertainties inherent in fulfilling both aspects of our dual mandate.

I supported the FOMC's decision to hold rates steady at our last policy meeting in March. Growth has remained solid so far but has started to show some signs of slowing. Labor market conditions have remained stable through February, and progress on inflation has eased, but the outlook is uncertain. These conditions led me to favor holding the policy rate constant at what I view as a moderately restrictive level.

The longer-term perspective provided by figure 9 shows that the FOMC responded to elevated inflation in the post-pandemic period by raising the policy rate 5-1/4 percentage points over about 15 months, starting in March 2022. After the Committee held the rate at that restrictive level for more than a year, progress on inflation allowed it to lower its policy rate by 1 full percentage point last year to its current level. The outcome of inflation moderating toward the 2 percent target without a large increase in unemployment was historically unusual but greatly welcomed.

Thinking about the future path of policy, I will continue to assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks. As we emphasize, monetary policy is not on a preset course. If the economy remains strong and inflation does not continue to move sustainably toward 2 percent, the current policy restraint could be retained for longer. If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, policy could be eased accordingly. In my view, there is no need to be in a hurry to make further policy rate adjustments. The current policy stance is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

output: In the early years of the switch to the new facilities, there were signs that healthy depository institutions became more willing to borrow from the discount window. This passage serves as an introduction to the 2025 community banking research conference. It is worth noting that the speaker expresses regret about not being able to attend in person while also recognizing the significant contributions this conference has made in advancing research related to community banking and its associated issues.

Since its inception in 2013, the conference has effectively synthesized insights from academic research, regulatory bodies, and the banking sector, all aimed at deepening the understanding of the community bank business model. This effort is intended to better inform future policy decisions in the field.

Additionally, the speaker, who has served as the former Kansas state bank commissioner as well as a community banker, expresses appreciation for the conference's objectives. This year, the organizers have once again curated valuable research and developed a program featuring a broad array of perspectives that facilitate discussion and debate among participants.

Furthermore, ensuring the future and viability of the community banking sector remains a critical priority, particularly in light of the recent appointment of the speaker as Vice Chair for Supervision of the Federal Reserve Board by the President.

This particular role, established under the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, involves the responsibility to develop policy recommendations for the Board regarding the supervision and regulation of depository institution holding companies and other financial entities under its supervision. It also entails overseeing the regulatory compliance of these firms.

Ultimately, the speaker conveys an immense sense of honor and privilege in being entrusted with these significant responsibilities. The speaker looks forward to collaborating with stakeholders across the financial industry to modernize the regulatory and supervisory frameworks, which can foster continued economic growth and innovation within the banking system while enhancing the vital role of community banks.
output:
Welcome to the 2025 community banking research conference. While I regret that I cannot join you in person this year, I would like to take a moment to acknowledge the contributions this conference has made and continues to make in promoting research on community banking and related issues.

Since 2013, this conference has synthesized insights and perspectives from research and regulatory and banking communities with a single goal: deepening our understanding of the community bank business model in order to better inform future policy decisions.

As the former Kansas state bank commissioner and a community banker, I very much appreciate the goals of this conference. And again this year, the organizers have included valuable research and created a conference program that includes a wide range of perspectives that create an opportunity for discussion and debate.

Ensuring the future and viability of the community banking industry continues to be a top priority, especially as the President appointed me to serve as the Vice Chair for Supervision of the Federal Reserve Board.

This position, which was created under the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, requires the Vice Chair to "develop policy recommendations for the Board regarding supervision and regulation of depository institution holding companies and other financial firms supervised by the Board" and to also "oversee the supervision and regulation" of these firms.

It is an honor and an absolute privilege to be entrusted with these important responsibilities, and I look forward to working with all of our stakeholders in the financial industry to modernize supervision and regulation that allows for continued economic growth and innovation in the banking system and that enhances the critical role of community banks.

In the supervisory process, it is essential to maintain focus and avoid distractions from less relevant issues. Additionally, the frequency of supervisory findings related to nonfinancial metrics may be influenced by the time required to address certain issues. This observation raises the question of whether this trend reflects a broader supervisory emphasis that shifts attention from financial risks to non-financial risks and internal processes, a shift that may warrant careful evaluation regarding its appropriateness. Furthermore, it is important to recognize the significant diversity in business models, sizes, and geographical presence among banks, suggesting that uniform standards may not be applicable to every institution. It is crucial to avoid the imposition of uniformity through approaches such as "grading on a curve," as this risk can be heightened during horizontal reviews. Notably, the supervisory findings generated during examinations play a critical role in determining bank ratings, which can subsequently impact various aspects of bank operations, including restrictions on mergers and acquisitions, increased liquidity costs, and the potential diversion of resources from other vital management priorities.

Moreover, guidance issued to banks can often incur costs that may not be immediately apparent or quantifiable. The primary objective of guidance is to enhance clarity for banks while reducing uncertainty and risk during implementation. However, for guidance to effectively achieve its intended purpose, it must be clear, actionable, and responsive to the specific needs of the targeted institutions, particularly community banks. Ultimately, ensuring effective guidance and supervision can contribute to the overall stability and functionality of the banking sector.
output:
In the supervisory process, we should guard against being distracted by less relevant issues. The prevalence of supervisory findings related to nonfinancial metrics is in part driven by the time it may take to remediate certain issues. However, we should also scrutinize whether this trend is indicative of our supervisory focus—beyond financial risk and toward non-financial risks and internal processes—and whether that shift is appropriate. We should also be aware that due to the vast diversity in business models, size, and geographic footprint among banks, we should not expect every firm to follow the same standards and must be careful to prevent forcing uniformity through "grading on a curve." This risk can be exacerbated through any type of horizontal-like reviews. The supervisory findings made during the examination process inform bank ratings, which can have follow-on effects like limiting options for mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity; raising the cost of liquidity; or diverting resources away from other, more important bank management priorities.

Guidance can also impose costs on banks that are not always obvious or quantified. The purpose of guidance is to provide clarity to banks and reduce implementation uncertainty and risk. To serve this purpose, however, guidance must be clear, actionable, and account for the needs of the targeted firms, especially for community banks.

Payroll employment growth may serve as an indicator of labor market momentum and can often help identify shifts in the path of the unemployment rate. When payroll gains are strong relative to trend labor force growth, they tend to point toward a lower unemployment rate and stronger labor market conditions, whereas weak payroll gains can often point toward a higher unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, because these data can be volatile or unreliable for a variety of reasons, closer attention tends to be paid to average payroll gains over a few months, which helps in understanding whether the labor market is moving closer to or further away from full employment.

Additionally, a multitude of other data is examined, both from the employment report and from other public and private surveys, in order to assess momentum and slack in the labor market. Regarding slack, data on discouraged and marginally attached workers and on involuntary part-time employment can indicate the extent of hidden unemployment and fragile employment. Furthermore, data on wage growth can help assess the relative strength of labor demand and supply, and the ratio of vacancies to unemployment also serves as a measure of labor market tightness. Regarding momentum, the composition of job gains by industry tends to indicate the breadth and depth of employment gains, and the payroll data are adjusted for persistent bias or expected revisions. Notably, indicators of layoffs, such as unemployment insurance claims, can detect early signs of a pickup in unemployment, and data on job openings also provide a signal about the strength of labor demand.

Regarding price stability, or inflation, the FOMC established 2 percent as the inflation goal in 2012, as measured by the annual change in the PCE price index. Consequently, policymakers closely monitor the recent path of total PCE inflation and how it is expected to evolve going forward. Ultimately, these various indicators together provide a broad framework for assessing labor market conditions and the outlook for inflation.

Additionally, community banks, in a manner similar to all banking institutions, are frequently required to obtain regulatory approval in order to engage in certain business activities and mergers, or to undertake new activities. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the process of applying for such regulatory approval appears to have become uncertain, cumbersome, disruptive, and slow in recent years.

Moreover, in some instances, application forms may fail to require a bank to submit the necessary information that is needed in order to evaluate an application properly. Additionally, the application process can often include standards that appear to make little sense when they are applied to community banks, such as the use of restrictive screens for evaluating the competitive effects of mergers in rural and underserved communities.

Furthermore, the process tends to lack specific action timelines that are necessary for business planning purposes. It is worth noting that mergers and acquisitions involve the coordination of a number of time-dependent processes, including transaction closing and staffing related planning, as well as the process of scheduling technology integrations with specialized vendors. In essence, the missing of deadlines can often be costly for the institutions involved, and we are currently working to improve this process by addressing these and other challenges, especially for community banks.

Additionally, I would like to discuss transparency, which I view as a critical element of the regulatory and supervisory processes. Furthermore, transparency in supervisory expectations appears to be just as important as transparency in regulatory requirements, and yet it often tends to receive the least scrutiny and attention.

Moreover, in part, the lack of transparency for supervision may result from information security rules and the manner in which they apply to communication between banks and examiners. It is worth noting that these have been protected from public scrutiny under the broad categorization of confidential supervisory information (CSI). Ultimately, the labeling of information as CSI tends to result in significant restrictions on its disclosure, and banks and bank employees may be subject to criminal penalties if they disclose CSI without regulatory approval, even if doing so would serve beneficial purposes for bank safety and soundness.

Like all banks, community banks often require regulatory approval to engage in some business activities and mergers, or to engage in new activities. The process of applying for regulatory approval has become uncertain, cumbersome, disruptive, and slow.

In some cases, application forms may not require a bank to submit the necessary information needed to evaluate an application. The application process may also include standards that make little sense when applied to community banks, like using restrictive screens for evaluating the competitive effects of mergers in rural and underserved communities.

In addition, the process often lacks specific action timelines necessary for business planning purposes. Mergers and acquisitions involve coordinating a number of time-dependent processes, including transaction closing and staffing related planning, and the process of scheduling technology integrations with specialized vendors. Missing deadlines can be costly for the institutions involved, and we are currently working to improve this process by addressing these and other challenges, especially for community banks.

Transparency Finally, I would like to discuss transparency, which I see as a critical element of the regulatory and supervisory processes. Transparency in supervisory expectations is just as important as transparency in regulatory requirements, and yet it often receives the least scrutiny and attention.

In part, the lack of transparency for supervision results from information security rules and how they apply to communication between banks and examiners. These have been protected from public scrutiny under the broad categorization of "confidential supervisory information" (CSI). Labeling information as CSI results in significant restrictions on its disclosure—banks and bank employees are subject to criminal penalties if they disclose CSI without regulatory approval even if doing so would serve beneficial purposes for bank safety and soundness.

The algorithms NIST has standardized are based on different math problems that would stymie both conventional and quantum computers.

In Gaithersburg, Maryland, it is worth noting that Laurie E. Locascio, who serves as the under secretary of commerce for standards and technology as well as the director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), has achieved a significant accolade by being elected to the National Academy of Engineering, which is regarded as one of the highest professional distinctions in the engineering field. 

Furthermore, Locascio is at the forefront of NIST’s collaborative initiatives that engage industry, academia, and government sectors with the aim of promoting United States innovation through enhancements in technology, measurements, and standards. A primary focus of her efforts is the effective execution of the CHIPS for America initiative, which comprises a $50 billion array of programs designed to reinforce and revitalize the leadership of the United States in semiconductor research, development, and manufacturing.

Additionally, Locascio is actively working to expand NIST’s involvement in critical emerging technologies, which include artificial intelligence, quantum information science, cybersecurity, privacy, biotechnology, energy, and advanced communications. It is notable that she also plays a significant role in fostering NIST’s ongoing contributions to the development of federal and international standards, which can often help to ensure the economic competitiveness and technological leadership of the United States.

Before her confirmation as NIST director in April 2022, Locascio held the position of vice president for research at both the University of Maryland College Park and the University of Maryland Baltimore. Prior to this, she dedicated 31 years to NIST, commencing her career as a research biomedical engineer and ultimately leading the agency’s Material Measurement Laboratory. Additionally, she held the position of acting associate director for laboratory programs, which is recognized as the second highest role within NIST, where she provided direction and operational guidance for the agency’s research initiatives.

In terms of her contributions to academia, Locascio has authored a total of 115 scientific papers and has been granted 12 patents in the domains of bioengineering and analytical chemistry. Notably, she holds membership as a fellow in several prestigious organizations, including the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Chemical Society, the American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering, and the National Academy of Inventors. Overall, Locascio's extensive experience and accomplishments highlight her significant impact in the fields of engineering and technology.
output:
Laurie E. Locascio, under secretary of commerce for standards and technology and director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), has been elected to the National Academy of Engineering — one of the highest professional distinctions accorded to an engineer.

Locascio leads NIST’s collaborative efforts with industry, academia and government to unleash U.S. innovation by advancing technology, measurements and standards. A key priority for her is the successful implementation of the CHIPS for America initiative, a $50 billion suite of programs to strengthen and revitalize U.S. leadership in semiconductor research, development and manufacturing.

In addition, Locascio is working to advance and grow NIST’s work in critical emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum information science, cybersecurity and privacy, biotechnology, energy and advanced communications. She also promotes NIST’s continuing role in advancing federal and international standards, which helps ensure U.S. economic competitiveness and technology leadership.

Before being confirmed as NIST director in April 2022, Locascio served as vice president for research at the University of Maryland College Park and University of Maryland Baltimore. Prior to that, she worked at NIST for 31 years, starting as a research biomedical engineer and rising to lead the agency’s Material Measurement Laboratory. She also served as the acting associate director for laboratory programs, the No. 2 position at NIST, providing direction and operational guidance for NIST’s research programs.

Locascio has published 115 scientific papers and has received 12 patents in the fields of bioengineering and analytical chemistry. She is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Chemical Society, the American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering, and the National Academy of Inventors.

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that Victoria Olson, who serves as the CDC’s deputy director of laboratory science and safety, has stated that positive control materials can often be critical for ensuring the reliability of diagnostic tests. Furthermore, she indicated that having a reliable supply of high-quality control material from a trusted source such as NIST may help the agency mount an effective testing program more quickly. In essence, the NIST control material is a liquid solution that contains partial sequences from nine mpox genes, which are strung together into molecules of DNA that are roughly 3,400 base pairs, or letter pairs, long. Notably, the value of the NIST control material does not tend to reside in the DNA itself, which is relatively easy to synthesize. Rather, it appears to reside in NIST’s assurance that each vial of the material contains the same very precisely measured amount of DNA, to a known degree of certainty. To illustrate, each microliter tends to contain 110,000 copies of the DNA strand, plus or minus 10 percent. Additionally, NIST scientists analyzed the DNA in order to ensure that there are no errors in the genetic sequences. Furthermore, they measured the concentration of DNA in the material through the use of a high-precision technique that is called digital PCR. Researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have developed a new device that may significantly enhance the process of converting heat into electricity. If this technology is further refined, it can potentially help recover some of the heat energy that is lost in the United States, which amounts to approximately $100 billion annually.

Notably, the innovative fabrication technique, which has been introduced by NIST researcher Kris Bertness along with her colleagues, involves the deposition of numerous microscopic columns made from gallium nitride on a silicon wafer. Subsequently, layers of silicon are removed from the bottom side of the wafer, leaving behind only a thin sheet of the material. The interaction between the columns and the silicon sheet tends to slow down the heat transfer within the silicon, thereby enabling a greater portion of the heat to be converted into electrical current. Bertness and her team from the University of Colorado Boulder shared their findings in the journal Advanced Materials on March 23.

Once this fabrication method reaches its full potential, it is conceivable that the silicon sheets could be applied around steam or exhaust pipes, allowing for the conversion of heat emissions into electricity that may be used to power nearby devices or integrated into a power grid. Furthermore, another possible application could involve the cooling of computer chips.

In essence, the study conducted by NIST and the University of Colorado is grounded in an intriguing phenomenon first identified by the German physicist Thomas Seebeck. During the early 1820s, Seebeck was investigating two metal wires, each composed of different materials, which were connected at both ends to form a loop. It is worth noting that when the two junctions of the wires were maintained at differing temperatures, a nearby compass needle exhibited a deflection. Subsequent researchers realized that this deflection occurred as a result of the temperature difference inducing a voltage between the two sections, leading to a flow of current from the hotter area to the cooler one. This current subsequently generated a magnetic field, which caused the compass needle to deflect. Ultimately, this historical discovery lays the foundation for the modern advancements being explored in heat-to-electricity conversion technology.

input: The U.S. Department of Commerce’s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has reached an agreement with the University of Vermont (UVM) to establish a Climate Measurements Center of Excellence, and this cooperative arrangement includes an award of $2.7 million that was appropriated by Congress for the purpose. Furthermore, the agreement was reached following a competitive process that was announced earlier this year, and it appears to reflect a broader effort to strengthen the scientific foundation for climate adaptation. Notably, Chuck Romine, the associate director for laboratory programs at NIST, said that the goal is to advance trust in measurements and technology in service to the nation, and he noted that effective measurements are key to understanding the dynamics of complex climate systems. In essence, he suggested that this center of excellence can amplify the agency’s impact and enable the development of equitable climate adaptation plans. Additionally, climate impacts tend to be experienced differently from one region of the U.S. to another, and communities often need more granular information than is currently available in order to develop adaptation plans. Furthermore, the Climate Measurements Center of Excellence is intended to support communities through the provision of standards frameworks, regional data, and the tools that communities need for decision-making. It is worth noting that climate impacts at the community level are expected to be diverse, complex, and interrelated, and examples of possible impacts include diminished agricultural productivity, poor air quality, increased food costs, supply chain and commercial logistics disruptions, and public health issues. Ultimately, preparing for and mitigating these impacts can often be challenging for any one community alone, so the center will bring local climate researchers together for the sharing of resources and ideas. In addition, it will serve as a hub for stakeholders including government climate offices, universities, nonprofits, industry, and NIST, and this collaborative structure tends to support more coordinated responses. In summary, the new center appears designed to combine federal investment, regional data, and stakeholder collaboration in support of more informed community climate adaptation.
output:

The encryption algorithms that NIST has announced today are detailed within the initial set of completed standards derived from NIST’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standardization project, and they are available for immediate application.

Furthermore, these three new standards are designed with a forward-looking perspective. This development poses significant risks to the security and privacy of individuals, organizations, and nations alike.

A novel technique for imaging concealed objects, developed by a researcher at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) together with his colleagues, may well diminish the enjoyment associated with games such as hide-and-seek, yet it also appears to offer significant potential for saving lives. The capacity to image scenes located beyond an observer's direct line of sight can often greatly enhance search and rescue missions, for example the location of a lost child within an abandoned factory, and it may likewise strengthen military and police surveillance operations, such as the exposure of a hidden terrorist or an enemy stronghold. Furthermore, the ability to see around corners and to reconstruct a complete image of a concealed object or obstacle in real time could someday contribute to improvements in robotic vision as well as in the safety and accuracy of self-driving cars, although it is worth noting that the prototype method cannot presently generate an image instantaneously.

Most conventional approaches to imaging objects behind an obstruction tend to rely on an external light source, such as ultra-short pulses of visible or infrared laser light. In essence, the light source initially illuminates a wall that scatters the light into the concealed region, and when the light subsequently strikes a hidden object, the object re-scatters a portion of that light back to the wall, where detection can then occur.

However, the imaging of hidden objects through the use of visible and infrared light alone is often challenging. At those relatively short wavelengths, a typical wall, regardless of how smooth it may appear to the human touch, presents itself as a rough surface and consequently scatters incoming light in all directions. As a result, it reveals less information about objects than light reflected from a smooth or mirrored surface would provide, and it requires sophisticated algorithms together with significant computing time to produce even a semi-sharp image. Additionally, the illumination may tip off adversaries that they are under surveillance. Ultimately, the proposed method appears to offer notable advantages over conventional approaches, even though further development is likely required before its full potential can be realized.

These mothers, instead of being able to work for their honest livelihood, are forced to employ all their time in stroling to beg sustenance for their helpless infants who, as they grow up, either turn thieves for want of work, or leave their dear native country, to fight for the Pretender in Spain, or sell themselves to the Barbadoes.

An enormous puppy gazed down at her with large, round eyes, and feebly extended one paw, attempting to make contact with her. Barely aware of her actions, she picked up a small stick and offered it to the puppy. Consequently, the puppy leaped into the air, propelling itself off all four feet simultaneously with a delighted yelp, and rushed towards the stick, feigning an intent to worry it. Alice, perceiving the situation as reminiscent of engaging in play with a cart-horse and anticipating the imminent possibility of being trampled, circled back around the thistle. Subsequently, the puppy initiated a series of brief charges toward the stick, moving only a short distance forward each time while retreating a considerable distance back, all the while barking hoarsely. output:

Hardly knowing what she did, she picked up a little bit of stick, and held it out to the puppy; whereupon the puppy jumped into the air off all its feet at once, with a yelp of delight, and rushed at the stick, and made believe to worry it; then Alice dodged behind a great thistle, to keep herself from being run over; and the moment she appeared on the other side, the puppy made another rush at the stick, and tumbled head over heels in its hurry to get hold of it; then Alice, thinking it was very like having a game of play with a cart-horse, and expecting every moment to be trampled under its feet, ran round the thistle again; then the puppy began a series of short charges at the stick, running a very little way forwards each time and a long way back, and barking hoarsely all the while, till at last it sat down a good way off, panting, with its tongue hanging out of its mouth, and its great eyes half shut.

input: The eyes of moles and certain burrowing rodents are rudimentary in size, and in some cases they are entirely covered by skin and fur. This condition of the eyes is probably the result of gradual reduction through disuse, although it may also have been aided by natural selection. In South America, a burrowing rodent known as the tuco-tuco, or Ctenomys, is even more subterranean in its habits than the mole. A Spaniard who had often caught these animals assured me that they were frequently blind. One that I kept alive was certainly in this condition, and dissection showed that the cause was inflammation of the nictitating membrane. Since frequent inflammation of the eyes must be harmful to any animal, and since eyes are certainly not indispensable to animals with subterranean habits, a reduction in their size, together with the adhesion of the eyelids and the growth of fur over them, might in such a case be an advantage. If this were so, natural selection would constantly aid the effects of disuse.

input: This highlights the observation that we know nothing about the origin or history of any of our domestic breeds. In reality, a breed, much like a dialect of a language, can hardly be said to have had a definite origin. A man preserves and breeds from an individual with some slight deviation of structure, or takes more care than usual in matching his best animals, thereby improving them, and the improved individuals slowly spread in the immediate neighbourhood. At this stage, however, they will hardly have a distinct name, and since they are only slightly valued, their history will be disregarded. When further improved through the same slow and gradual process, they will spread more widely and come to be recognised as something distinct and valuable, and will then probably first receive a provincial name. In semi-civilised countries with little free communication, the spreading and knowledge of any new sub-breed will be a slow process. Once the points of value of the new sub-breed are fully acknowledged, the principle of unconscious selection will always tend to slowly add to the characteristic features of the breed, whatever they may be, perhaps more at one period than another as the breed rises or falls in fashion, and perhaps more in one district than another according to the state of civilisation of the inhabitants. Ultimately, the chance of any record having been preserved of such slow, varying, and insensible changes will be infinitely small.

input: It is important to note that the process may not occur as consistently as illustrated in the diagram, even if it is somewhat irregular. It is not necessarily the case that the most distinct varieties will always dominate and reproduce; a more moderate form may often persist for extended periods and might or might not lead to more than one altered descendant. Natural selection typically operates based on the specific characteristics of environments that are either unoccupied or not fully occupied by other organisms, which can be influenced by a multitude of complex interactions. Generally speaking, the more varied in structure the descendants from a single species can become, the better their chances of exploiting different niches, which may lead to an increase in their modified offspring. In the diagram, the line of succession appears to be interrupted at regular intervals, indicated by small numbered letters that represent the distinct forms recognized as varieties. However, these interruptions are theoretical and could have been placed at various points, assuming sufficient time for significant divergent variation to accumulate. Overall, the complexity of these processes highlights the nuanced nature of evolutionary change.
output: But I must here remark that I do not suppose that the process ever goes on so regularly as is represented in the diagram, though in itself made somewhat irregular. I am far from thinking that the most divergent varieties will invariably prevail and multiply: a medium form may often long endure, and may or may not produce more than one modified descendant; for natural selection will always act according to the nature of the places which are either unoccupied or not perfectly occupied by other beings; and this will depend on infinitely complex relations. But as a general rule, the more diversified in structure the descendants from any one species can be rendered, the more places they will be enabled to seize on, and the more their modified progeny will be increased. In our diagram the line of succession is broken at regular intervals by small numbered letters marking the successive forms which have become sufficiently distinct to be recorded as varieties. But these breaks are imaginary, and might have been inserted anywhere, after intervals long enough to have allowed the accumulation of a considerable amount of divergent variation.

input: This passage summarizes the conditions that can influence natural selection, focusing on both favorable and unfavorable factors. It suggests that a large continental area, which is likely to experience significant fluctuations in elevation, is conducive to the emergence of diverse life forms that may thrive and expand over time. Initially, when this area exists as a continent, its diverse population will face intense competition. As subsidence transforms the continent into separate islands, many individuals of the same species will remain on each island, leading to restricted interbreeding at the edges of their ranges. This isolation, coupled with any physical changes, will hinder immigration, necessitating that new ecological niches be filled by adaptations of existing species. Over time, these modifications can lead to well-defined varieties. Should the islands eventually be uplifted back into a continental form, competition will resurge, allowing the more advantageous varieties to proliferate. This process may result in the extinction of less adapted forms, altering the relative proportions of the continent's inhabitants and providing further opportunities for natural selection to drive the evolution of new species.
output: To sum up the circumstances favourable and unfavourable to natural selection, as far as the extreme intricacy of the subject permits. I conclude, looking to the future, that for terrestrial productions a large continental area, which will probably undergo many oscillations of level, and which consequently will exist for long periods in a broken condition, will be the most favourable for the production of many new forms of life, likely to endure long and to spread widely. For the area will first have existed as a continent, and the inhabitants, at this period numerous in individuals and kinds, will have been subjected to very severe competition. When converted by subsidence into large separate islands, there will still exist many individuals of the same species on each island: intercrossing on the confines of the range of each species will thus be checked: after physical changes of any kind, immigration will be prevented, so that new places in the polity of each island will have to be filled up by modifications of the old inhabitants; and time will be allowed for the varieties in each to become well modified and perfected. When, by renewed elevation, the islands shall be re-converted into a continental area, there will again be severe competition: the most favoured or improved varieties will be enabled to spread: there will be much extinction of the less improved forms, and the relative proportional numbers of the various inhabitants of the renewed continent will again be changed; and again there will be a fair field for natural selection to improve still further the inhabitants, and thus produce new species.

Conversely, these observations could appear puzzling if species were created independently while varieties were formed through secondary processes. Ultimately, this raises important questions about the nature of species and varieties in the context of their relationships and origins.
output: If species be only well-marked and permanent varieties, we can at once see why their crossed offspring should follow the same complex laws in their degrees and kinds of resemblance to their parents, - in being absorbed into each other by successive crosses, and in other such points, - as do the crossed offspring of acknowledged varieties. On the other hand, these would be strange facts if species have been independently created, and varieties have been produced by secondary laws.
title: On the Origin of Species

input: The observations discussed indicate that the composition of legislative bodies is primarily influenced by the interests and perspectives of various community classes. Strong individuals from all backgrounds can overcome challenges posed by their circumstances and gain recognition for their abilities, receiving respect from both their specific groups and society at large. However, such instances do not undermine the reasoning based on the prevailing patterns observed.
output: WE HAVE seen that the result of the observations, to which the foregoing number has been principally devoted, is, that from the natural operation of the different interests and views of the various classes of the community, whether the representation of the people be more or less numerous, it will consist almost entirely of proprietors of land, of merchants, and of members of the learned professions, who will truly represent all those different interests and views. If it should be objected that we have seen other descriptions of men in the local legislatures, I answer that it is admitted there are exceptions to the rule, but not in sufficient number to influence the general complexion or character of the government. There are strong minds in every walk of life that will rise superior to the disadvantages of situation, and will command the tribute due to their merit, not only from the classes to which they particularly belong, but from the society in general. The door ought to be equally open to all; and I trust, for the credit of human nature, that we shall see examples of such vigorous plants flourishing in the soil of federal as well as of State legislation; but occasional instances of this sort will not render the reasoning founded upon the general course of things, less conclusive.

This tends to be especially true with regard to operations in the West Indies. A few ships of the line, sent at the right time to reinforce either side, could often be enough to determine the outcome of a campaign, and matters of the greatest importance might depend on that outcome. Our position in this respect is a very strong one. If we also consider how useful supplies from this country can be in carrying out military operations in the West Indies, it can readily be seen that such a favorable situation would allow us to negotiate with considerable advantage for commercial privileges. A price could be placed not only on our friendship but also on our neutrality. By steadily adhering to the Union, we may hope before long to become the arbiter of Europe in America and to be able to tilt the balance of European rivalries in this part of the world as our interests may require.
output: A further resource for influencing the conduct of European nations toward us, in this respect, would arise from the establishment of a federal navy. Common sense indicates that a power that has sought to conquer us is not the most appropriate choice for our defense. This highlights the potential for conquest to occur under the guise of friendship, risking that, after a prolonged and courageous struggle, we could be deceived into a state of subjugation. If British ships are not allowed in our harbors, one might wonder how they could effectively safeguard us. A navy located three or four thousand miles away would have limited utility, particularly during urgent situations. Ultimately, if we must defend ourselves, it stands to reason that we should do so independently rather than relying on another nation.
output: Some, perhaps, will say, that after we have made it up with Britain, she will protect us. Can we be so unwise as to mean, that she shall keep a navy in our harbours for that purpose? Common sense will tell us, that the power which hath endeavoured to subdue us, is of all others, the most improper to defend us. Conquest may be effected under the pretence of friendship; and ourselves, after a long and brave resistance, be at last cheated into slavery. And if her ships are not to be admitted into our harbours, I would ask, how is she to protect us? A navy three or four thousand miles off can be of little use, and on sudden emergencies, none at all. Wherefore, if we must hereafter protect ourselves, why not do it for ourselves? Why do it for another?
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The contest for the monarchy and succession, between the Houses of York and Lancaster, subjected England to a prolonged period of violence. Over the course of this conflict, twelve major battles, in addition to various skirmishes and sieges, were waged between Henry and Edward. On two occasions, Henry was taken captive by Edward, only to find himself in a similar position at the hands of Henry. Furthermore, the unpredictable nature of warfare and the sentiments of a nation are evident, particularly when personal disputes serve as the foundation for conflict. This is illustrated by the fact that Henry was triumphantly escorted from a prison to a palace, while Edward was compelled to flee from a palace to a foreign land. However, as is often the case with abrupt changes in fortune, such transitions are rarely enduring; thus, Henry was ultimately displaced from the throne, and Edward was reinstated to succeed him. It is worth noting that Parliament consistently aligned itself with the faction that appeared strongest.
output: The contest for monarchy and succession, between the houses of York and Lancaster, laid England in a scene of blood for many years. Twelve pitched battles, besides skirmishes and sieges, were fought between Henry and Edward. Twice was Henry prisoner to Edward, who in his turn was prisoner to Henry. And so uncertain is the fate of war and the temper of a nation, when nothing but personal matters are the ground of a quarrel, that Henry was taken in triumph from a prison to a palace, and Edward obliged to fly from a palace to a foreign land; yet, as sudden transitions of temper are seldom lasting, Henry in his turn was driven from the throne, and Edward recalled to succeed him. The parliament always following the strongest side.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Immediate necessity can render certain actions convenient, but if such actions continue unchecked, they may lead to oppression. It is important to distinguish between expedience and what is right. During the crises that America faced, the appointment of representatives from various Houses of Assembly was a practical and appropriate solution for consultation, and this approach helped to protect the continent from disaster. However, it is likely that a Congress will always be in existence, and it is essential for those invested in maintaining order to consider how its members are chosen. This raises a question for those who study human behavior: is it wise for a single group of individuals to hold both representation and election powers? As we plan for future generations, it is crucial to recognize that virtue is not something that can be inherited.
output: Immediate necessity makes many things convenient, which if continued would grow into oppressions. Expedience and right are different things. When the calamities of America required a consultation, there was no method so ready, or at that time so proper, as to appoint persons from the several Houses of Assembly for that purpose; and the wisdom with which they have proceeded hath preserved this continent from ruin. But as it is more than probable that we shall never be without a Congress, every well wisher to good order, must own, that the mode for choosing members of that body, deserves consideration. And I put it as a question to those, who make a study of mankind, whether representation and election is not too great a power for one and the same body of men to possess? When we are planning for posterity, we ought to remember, that virtue is not hereditary.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

output:
To say that the constitution of England is a union of three powers reciprocally checking each other, is farcical, either the words have no meaning, or they are flat contradictions.

First. - That the king is not to be trusted without being looked after, or in other words, that a thirst for absolute power is the natural disease of monarchy.

Secondly. - That the commons, by being appointed for that purpose, are either wiser or more worthy of confidence than the crown.

input: Human beings may have started as equals in the process of creation, and this equality could only have been altered by later circumstances. The differences between wealth and poverty can often be explained, perhaps without needing to resort to the more severe terms of oppression and greed. While oppression can frequently be a result of wealth disparities, it is rarely the direct cause of them. Additionally, while greed may help someone avoid severe financial hardship, it often makes them too cautious to achieve true wealth. In summary, the dynamics of equality and wealth are complex and influenced by various factors.
output: Mankind being originally equals in the order of creation, the equality could only be destroyed by some subsequent circumstance; the distinctions of rich, and poor, may in a great measure be accounted for, and that without having recourse to the harsh ill sounding names of oppression and avarice. Oppression is often the consequence, but seldom or never the means of riches; and though avarice will preserve a man from being necessitously poor, it generally makes him too timorous to be wealthy.
