author: Frederick Douglass

input: This mode of treatment exemplifies the broader system of deception and cruelty associated with slavery. It highlights how the approach taken seeks to instill a revulsion toward freedom by exposing the enslaved individuals only to its negative aspects. A notable example is when a slave, who has a fondness for molasses, steals some. In many instances, the master then goes to town and purchases a large quantity. Upon returning, the master forces the slave to consume the molasses until he becomes sickened by it. This method is similarly applied to discourage slaves from requesting more food than their standard allowance. When a slave exhausts his ration and seeks additional food, the master often reacts with anger but, rather than sending the slave away hungry, provides an excessive amount and mandates consumption within a specific timeframe. If the slave then expresses difficulty in eating the food, he may be punished for being discontented, as he is deemed neither satisfied nor fasting. This suggests a broader pattern of punitive measures aimed at controlling the desires and actions of enslaved individuals. The examples provided illustrate a prevalent practice within this system.
output: I have said that this mode of treatment is a part of the whole system of fraud and inhumanity of slavery. It is so. The mode here adopted to disgust the slave with freedom, by allowing him to see only the abuse of it, is carried out in other things. For instance, a slave loves molasses; he steals some. His master, in many cases, goes off to town, and buys a large quantity; he returns, takes his whip, and commands the slave to eat the molasses, until the poor fellow is made sick at the very mention of it. The same mode is sometimes adopted to make the slaves refrain from asking for more food than their regular allowance. A slave runs through his allowance, and applies for more. His master is enraged at him; but, not willing to send him off without food, gives him more than is necessary, and compels him to eat it within a given time. Then, if he complains that he cannot eat it, he is said to be satisfied neither full nor fasting, and is whipped for being hard to please! I have an abundance of such illustrations of the same principle, drawn from my own observation, but think the cases I have cited sufficient. The practice is a very common one.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: The reader may consider me a hopeless busybody when I admit how much this man stimulated my curiosity and how often I tried to break through the reticence he showed concerning himself. Before passing judgment, however, one should remember how aimless my life was and how little there was to occupy my attention. My health prevented me from going out unless the weather was exceptionally mild, and I had no friends who would visit me and interrupt the monotony of my daily existence. Under these circumstances, I eagerly welcomed the small mystery surrounding my companion and spent much of my time attempting to unravel it.
output: The reader may set me down as a hopeless busybody, when I confess how much this man stimulated my curiosity, and how often I endeavoured to break through the reticence which he showed on all that concerned himself. Before pronouncing judgment, however, be it remembered, how objectless was my life, and how little there was to engage my attention. My health forbade me from venturing out unless the weather was exceptionally genial, and I had no friends who would call upon me and break the monotony of my daily existence. Under these circumstances, I eagerly hailed the little mystery which hung around my companion, and spent much of my time in endeavouring to unravel it.
title: A Study in Scarlet
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input: Jefferson Hope suggested that it may be advisable to start immediately, speaking in a calm yet determined tone that indicated his awareness of the serious danger they faced. He noted that while the front and back entrances are being monitored, it might be possible to escape through the side window and navigate across the fields with care. Once they reach the road, it is likely that they would only be a couple of miles from the Ravine where the horses are waiting. By daybreak, they could potentially be halfway through the mountains. Overall, the plan seems feasible if they proceed cautiously.
output: “We must make our start at once,” said Jefferson Hope, speaking in a low but resolute voice, like one who realizes the greatness of the peril, but has steeled his heart to meet it. “The front and back entrances are watched, but with caution we may get away through the side window and across the fields. Once on the road we are only two miles from the Ravine where the horses are waiting. By daybreak we should be half-way through the mountains.”
title: A Study in Scarlet
author: Arthur Conan Doyle

input: With the stigma lifted, Hester experienced a profound release, as the burdens of shame and anguish lifted from her spirit. This highlights the significant relief she felt, which she had not fully recognized until she experienced the freedom. Following this impulse, she removed the formal cap that had restricted her hair, allowing it to cascade over her shoulders, rich and dark, creating a contrast of shadow and light that softened her features. A radiant and tender smile emerged around her mouth and shone in her eyes, suggesting a deep connection to her femininity. A vibrant blush returned to her cheeks, which had long been pale. The aspects of her identity, including her youth and beauty, returned from what is often perceived as an irreversible past, merging with her youthful hope and an unfamiliar happiness in this moment. This signifies that the heaviness of the earth and sky dissipated alongside their sorrow. Suddenly, as if illuminated by a divine presence, sunlight broke through, flooding the previously shadowed forest, brightening each green leaf, transforming the yellow fallen leaves into gold, and illuminating the gray trunks of the trees. Objects that once cast shadows now embodied brightness. The path of the little brook could be traced by its joyful sparkle as it wound its way into the heart of the woods, which had transformed into a place of joy.
output: The stigma gone, Hester heaved a long, deep sigh, in which the burden of shame and anguish departed from her spirit. O exquisite relief! She had not known the weight, until she felt the freedom! By another impulse, she took off the formal cap that confined her hair; and down it fell upon her shoulders, dark and rich, with at once a shadow and a light in its abundance, and imparting the charm of softness to her features. There played around her mouth, and beamed out of her eyes, a radiant and tender smile, that seemed gushing from the very heart of womanhood. A crimson flush was glowing on her cheek, that had been long so pale. Her sex, her youth, and the whole richness of her beauty, came back from what men call the irrevocable past, and clustered themselves, with her maiden hope, and a happiness before unknown, within the magic circle of this hour. And, as if the gloom of the earth and sky had been but the effluence of these two mortal hearts, it vanished with their sorrow. All at once, as with a sudden smile of heaven, forth burst the sunshine, pouring a very flood into the obscure forest, gladdening each green leaf, transmuting the yellow fallen ones to gold, and gleaming adown the gray trunks of the solemn trees. The objects that had made a shadow hitherto, embodied the brightness now. The course of the little brook might be traced by its merry gleam afar into the wood’s heart of mystery, which had become a mystery of joy.
title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

input:
At times, a light flickered in the physician’s eyes, a burning blue that seemed foreboding, reminiscent of a furnace's glow. It was akin to the eerie flashes of fire that emerged from Bunyan’s terrifying doorway in the hillside, shimmering briefly on the face of the pilgrim. The ground where this dark miner was laboring may have revealed signs that fueled his determination. 

“This man,” he thought during one of these moments, “as pure as he appears, as spiritual as he seems, has inherited a potent animal nature from his parents. I will explore further in this direction.”
output:
Sometimes, a light glimmered out of the physician’s eyes, burning blue and ominous, like the reflection of a furnace, or, let us say, like one of those gleams of ghastly fire that darted from Bunyan’s awful doorway in the hillside, and quivered on the pilgrim’s face. The soil where this dark miner was working had perchance shown indications that encouraged him.

“This man,” said he, at one such moment, to himself, “pure as they deem him, - all spiritual as he seems, - hath inherited a strong animal nature from his father or his mother. Let us dig a little further in the direction of this vein!”
title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

input: What sets the physician's ecstasy apart from that of Satan is the presence of wonder within it. Following the recent incident, the interactions between the clergyman and the physician transformed in nature, although they appeared outwardly unchanged. Roger Chillingworth's intellect now had a clear direction, though it was not the path he had originally envisioned. While he maintained a calm, gentle demeanor, a quiet malice that had previously been hidden became active in this unfortunate old man. This suggests that he envisioned a form of revenge that was more intimate than any typically enacted by a mortal upon an enemy. He sought to become the trusted confidant to whom all fear, remorse, agony, and futile repentance could be revealed, along with the return of sinful thoughts that had been suppressed in vain. Ultimately, this hidden sorrow, which would have been met with compassion and forgiveness by the world, was intended to be laid bare before him, a figure characterized by a lack of empathy and forgiveness. This dark assortment of emotions would serve as a means to repay the debt of vengeance to the very individual who had wronged him.
output:
But what distinguished the physician’s ecstasy from Satan’s was the trait of wonder in it!

After the incident last described, the intercourse between the clergyman and the physician, though externally the same, was really of another character than it had previously been. The intellect of Roger Chillingworth had now a sufficiently plain path before it. It was not, indeed, precisely that which he had laid out for himself to tread. Calm, gentle, passionless, as he appeared, there was yet, we fear, a quiet depth of malice, hitherto latent, but active now, in this unfortunate old man, which led him to imagine a more intimate revenge than any mortal had ever wreaked upon an enemy. To make himself the one trusted friend, to whom should be confided all the fear, the remorse, the agony, the ineffectual repentance, the backward rush of sinful thoughts, expelled in vain! All that guilty sorrow, hidden from the world, whose great heart would have pitied and forgiven, to be revealed to him, the Pitiless, to him, the Unforgiving! All that dark treasure to be lavished on the very man, to whom nothing else could so adequately pay the debt of vengeance!
title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

input: The mariner informed Hester that he needed to arrange for an additional sleeping quarter beyond what had been agreed upon. He reassured her that there was no need for concern about scurvy or ship-related illnesses during the journey, as the presence of both a ship's surgeon and another doctor would mitigate health risks. He noted that the primary concern would be related to medications, especially since there was a significant supply of apothecary goods on board, which he had obtained through trade with a Spanish ship. Hester, taken aback by this news, asked for clarification, particularly regarding the possibility of an additional passenger.
output:
“So, mistress,” said the mariner, “I must bid the steward make ready one more berth than you bargained for! No fear of scurvy or ship-fever, this voyage! What with the ship’s surgeon and this other doctor, our only danger will be from drug or pill; more by token, as there is a lot of apothecary’s stuff aboard, which I traded for with a Spanish vessel.”

“What mean you?” inquired Hester, startled more than she permitted to appear. “Have you another passenger?”
title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

input: On this particular day, there may have been an expression that had never been observed before or, indeed, one that was not easily recognizable now; unless perhaps there existed an extraordinarily perceptive observer who could first understand her heart and then look for a related change in her face and demeanor. Such a sensitive soul might have believed that after enduring the scrutinizing gaze of the crowd for seven long years—viewed as a necessity, a punishment, and something akin to a harsh faith—she now willingly faced it one last time, aiming to transform her prolonged suffering into a sense of triumph. She might have quietly addressed the onlookers, saying, “Take a good look at the scarlet letter and its bearer! Soon, she will be out of your reach! In just a few hours, the profound and mysterious ocean will extinguish and conceal forever the mark you have forced upon her.” It may not be too far-fetched to imagine that Hester felt a twinge of regret as she was on the verge of gaining her freedom from a pain that had become entwined with her very existence. Could she not have experienced an overwhelming urge to savor one final, intense taste of the bitter experiences that had flavored most of her adult life? The future may hold for her a life that is rich, delightful, and invigorating, served in a beautiful golden cup; otherwise, it might leave her with an unavoidable weariness following the bitterness that had long been her companion.
output: It might be, on this one day, that there was an expression unseen before, nor, indeed, vivid enough to be detected now; unless some preternaturally gifted observer should have first read the heart, and have afterwards sought a corresponding development in the countenance and mien. Such a spiritual seer might have conceived, that, after sustaining the gaze of the multitude through seven miserable years as a necessity, a penance, and something which it was a stern religion to endure, she now, for one last time more, encountered it freely and voluntarily, in order to convert what had so long been agony into a kind of triumph. “Look your last on the scarlet letter and its wearer!” - the people’s victim and life-long bond-slave, as they fancied her, might say to them. “Yet a little while, and she will be beyond your reach! A few hours longer, and the deep, mysterious ocean will quench and hide forever the symbol which ye have caused to burn upon her bosom!” Nor were it an inconsistency too improbable to be assigned to human nature, should we suppose a feeling of regret in Hester’s mind, at the moment when she was about to win her freedom from the pain which had been thus deeply incorporated with her being. Might there not be an irresistible desire to quaff a last, long, breathless draught of the cup of wormwood and aloes, with which nearly all her years of womanhood had been perpetually flavored? The wine of life, henceforth to be presented to her lips, must be indeed rich, delicious, and exhilarating, in its chased and golden beaker; or else leave an inevitable and weary languor, after the lees of bitterness wherewith she had been drugged, as with a cordial of intensest potency.
title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

input: He looked darkly at the clergyman and said that even if he had searched the whole earth, there was no place so secret, no high place or lowly place, where he could have escaped him, except on this very scaffold. Yet he trembled and turned to Hester with an expression of doubt and anxiety in his eyes. This was all the more evident because a feeble smile remained on his lips. Partly supported by Hester Prynne and holding one hand of little Pearl, the Reverend Mr. Dimmesdale turned to the dignified and venerable rulers, to the holy ministers who were his brethren, and to the people, whose great heart was thoroughly appalled yet overflowing with tearful sympathy. They knew that some deep life-matter, which if full of sin was full of anguish and repentance likewise, was now to be laid open to them. The sun, but little past its meridian, shone down upon the clergyman and gave a distinctness to his figure as he stood out from all the earth to put in his plea of guilty at the bar of Eternal Justice.
output:
“Hadst thou sought the whole earth over,” said he, looking darkly at the clergyman, “there was no one place so secret, - no high place nor lowly place, where thou couldst have escaped me, - save on this very scaffold!”

Yet he trembled, and turned to Hester with an expression of doubt and anxiety in his eyes, not the less evidently betrayed, that there was a feeble smile upon his lips.

Partly supported by Hester Prynne, and holding one hand of little Pearl’s, the Reverend Mr. Dimmesdale turned to the dignified and venerable rulers; to the holy ministers, who were his brethren; to the people, whose great heart was thoroughly appalled, yet overflowing with tearful sympathy, as knowing that some deep life-matter - which, if full of sin, was full of anguish and repentance likewise - was now to be laid open to them. The sun, but little past its meridian, shone down upon the clergyman, and gave a distinctness to his figure, as he stood out from all the earth, to put in his plea of guilty at the bar of Eternal Justice.
title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

input: When a Sperm Whale is captured in the Southern Fishery, it is generally not customary to begin the process of cutting it up immediately, especially late at night. This task is extremely labor-intensive, does not conclude quickly, and requires the full attention of the crew. Consequently, the typical practice is to take in all sail and secure the helm, allowing the crew to rest in their hammocks until dawn. However, two crew members must remain on deck in rotation for an hour at a time to monitor the situation, ensuring that everything proceeds smoothly until morning.
output: When in the Southern Fishery, a captured Sperm Whale, after long and weary toil, is brought alongside late at night, it is not, as a general thing at least, customary to proceed at once to the business of cutting him in. For that business is an exceedingly laborious one; is not very soon completed; and requires all hands to set about it. Therefore, the common usage is to take in all sail; lash the helm a’lee; and then send every one below to his hammock till daylight, with the reservation that, until that time, anchor-watches shall be kept; that is, two and two for an hour, each couple, the crew in rotation shall mount the deck to see that all goes well.
title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
author: Herman Melville

input: Meanwhile, while supervising another section of the vessel, Captain Peleg vociferously expressed his frustrations from the stern in an alarming manner. I nearly believed he might cause the ship to capsize prior to the retrieval of the anchor; consequently, I found myself pausing with my handspike and instructed Queequeg to do likewise, reflecting on the dangers we both faced in embarking on our journey under the command of such a volatile pilot. Despite this, I reassured myself with the notion that there might be some hope in the pious Bildad, notwithstanding his seven hundred seventy-seventh sermon. However, my thoughts were abruptly interrupted by a sudden and sharp impact to my rear, and upon turning, I was appalled to discover Captain Peleg in the process of retracting his leg from my immediate vicinity. That experience marked my first encounter with physical reprimand.
output: Meantime, overseeing the other part of the ship, Captain Peleg ripped and swore astern in the most frightful manner. I almost thought he would sink the ship before the anchor could be got up; involuntarily I paused on my handspike, and told Queequeg to do the same, thinking of the perils we both ran, in starting on the voyage with such a devil for a pilot. I was comforting myself, however, with the thought that in pious Bildad might be found some salvation, spite of his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay; when I felt a sudden sharp poke in my rear, and turning round, was horrified at the apparition of Captain Peleg in the act of withdrawing his leg from my immediate vicinity. That was my first kick.
title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
author: Herman Melville

input: As evening approached, I felt reasonably certain that all of his activities and rituals had concluded, so I decided to check on him in his room. I knocked gently on the door, but received no response. Attempting to open it, I found it securely fastened from within. "Queequeg," I called softly through the keyhole, but there was only silence. "I say, Queequeg! Why don’t you respond? It’s me—Ishmael." Yet, the stillness persisted, which began to concern me. I had given him ample time, and it crossed my mind that he may have experienced a medical issue. Peering through the keyhole, I was met with an odd angle, which provided a rather limited view. I could see only part of the bed frame and a section of the wall, with no further insight. It caught my attention to see Queequeg’s harpoon resting against the wall. The landlady had taken it from him the previous evening before we went to our room. This struck me as unusual, yet since the harpoon was indeed there and he rarely ventured out without it, it seemed likely he was still inside.
output: Towards evening, when I felt assured that all his performances and rituals must be over, I went up to his room and knocked at the door; but no answer. I tried to open it, but it was fastened inside. “Queequeg,” said I softly through the key-hole: - all silent. “I say, Queequeg! why don’t you speak? It’s I - Ishmael.” But all remained still as before. I began to grow alarmed. I had allowed him such abundant time; I thought he might have had an apoplectic fit. I looked through the key-hole; but the door opening into an odd corner of the room, the key-hole prospect was but a crooked and sinister one. I could only see part of the foot-board of the bed and a line of the wall, but nothing more. I was surprised to behold resting against the wall the wooden shaft of Queequeg’s harpoon, which the landlady the evening previous had taken from him, before our mounting to the chamber. That’s strange, thought I; but at any rate, since the harpoon stands yonder, and he seldom or never goes abroad without it, therefore he must be inside here, and no possible mistake.
title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
author: Herman Melville

input: In essence, one must consider how, within this designated quest, Ahab fails to make contact with any land. Does his crew subsist solely on air? Surely, he must pause for water. However, this is not the case. For an extended period, the sun, akin to a circus performer, has traversed its fiery path, requiring no sustenance other than that which resides within itself. Thus, Ahab. Furthermore, it is important to observe the nature of the whaler. While other vessels are burdened with foreign goods destined for distant docks, the wandering whale ship carries only herself, her crew, their weapons, and their necessities. She contains the equivalent of an entire lake within her spacious hold. She is balanced with useful provisions rather than merely with unusable materials such as pig lead and kentledge. She retains years' worth of water. This water, sourced from the pristine wells of Nantucket, is preferred by the Nantucketer in the Pacific after three years at sea, over the brackish fluid acquired just the day before from the rivers of Peru or India. Thus, while other ships may have traveled from New York to China and back, stopping at numerous ports, the whale ship may not have encountered even a single grain of soil during that time; her crew having seen no one other than fellow sailors adrift like themselves. Consequently, if one were to inform them that another flood had occurred, they would merely respond, "Well, boys, here is the ark!"
output: But how now? in this zoned quest, does Ahab touch no land? does his crew drink air? Surely, he will stop for water. Nay. For a long time, now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring, and needs no sustenance but what’s in himself. So Ahab. Mark this, too, in the whaler. While other hulls are loaded down with alien stuff, to be transferred to foreign wharves; the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake’s contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with utilities; not altogether with unusable pig-lead and kentledge. She carries years’ water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water; which, when three years afloat, the Nantucketer, in the Pacific, prefers to drink before the brackish fluid, but yesterday rafted off in casks, from the Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is, that, while other ships may have gone to China from New York, and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship, in all that interval, may not have sighted one grain of soil; her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that did you carry them the news that another flood had come; they would only answer - “Well, boys, here’s the ark!”
title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
author: Herman Melville

input: This situation could not continue indefinitely; it seems unlikely that any horse could maintain its footing under such conditions, as the pain might be too significant. I tripped and fell rather hard on my knees. Smith was thrown off due to my fall, and given the speed at which I was moving, it is possible he landed quite forcefully. I managed to regain my feet and limped over to the edge of the road, where the ground was free of stones. The moon had just risen above the hedge, and in its light, I could see Smith lying a few yards away from me. He did not get up; he made a small attempt to do so but then let out a deep groan. I could have groaned as well, for I was experiencing considerable pain in both my foot and knees; however, horses tend to endure their discomfort quietly. I remained silent, standing still and listening. I heard another heavy groan from Smith; although he lay fully illuminated by the moon, I could not see any movement from him. Feeling helpless for both him and myself, I listened intently for the sound of a horse, wheels, or footsteps. The road was not heavily traveled, and at this hour, we might wait for quite some time before assistance arrived. I stood there, observing and listening. The night was calm and pleasant, with only the soft notes of a nightingale breaking the silence, and the only movement was from the white clouds near the moon and a brown owl that glided over the hedge. This scene reminded me of summer nights long ago, when I would lie beside my mother in the lovely green meadow at Farmer Grey's.
output: This could not go on; no horse could keep his footing under such circumstances; the pain was too great. I stumbled, and fell with violence on both my knees. Smith was flung off by my fall, and, owing to the speed I was going at, he must have fallen with great force. I soon recovered my feet and limped to the side of the road, where it was free from stones. The moon had just risen above the hedge, and by its light I could see Smith lying a few yards beyond me. He did not rise; he made one slight effort to do so, and then there was a heavy groan. I could have groaned, too, for I was suffering intense pain both from my foot and knees; but horses are used to bear their pain in silence. I uttered no sound, but I stood there and listened. One more heavy groan from Smith; but though he now lay in the full moonlight I could see no motion. I could do nothing for him nor myself, but, oh! how I listened for the sound of horse, or wheels, or footsteps! The road was not much frequented, and at this time of the night we might stay for hours before help came to us. I stood watching and listening. It was a calm, sweet April night; there were no sounds but a few low notes of a nightingale, and nothing moved but the white clouds near the moon and a brown owl that flitted over the hedge. It made me think of the summer nights long ago, when I used to lie beside my mother in the green pleasant meadow at Farmer Grey's.
title: Black Beauty
author: Anna Sewell

input: This highlights the importance of a gentle touch when handling horses, as it can contribute to their comfort, responsiveness, and overall temperament. Horses have sensitive mouths, which can respond to even the slightest adjustments made by the driver. When a horse's mouth has not been negatively affected by poor treatment, it can quickly understand the rider’s intentions. The speaker notes that their own mouth has remained unspoiled, which may explain the preference of their mistress over another horse named Ginger, despite Ginger's comparable abilities. Ginger often expressed frustration about her situation, attributing her less ideal mouth to the harsh training methods used in London. An older horse, Sir Oliver, reassured Ginger by pointing out that her strength and agility allowed her to carry a tall rider without needing to lower her head, suggesting that horses should accept their circumstances and remain willing as long as they are treated kindly.
output: Oh! if people knew what a comfort to horses a light hand is, and how it keeps a good mouth and a good temper, they surely would not chuck, and drag, and pull at the rein as they often do. Our mouths are so tender that where they have not been spoiled or hardened with bad or ignorant treatment, they feel the slightest movement of the driver's hand, and we know in an instant what is required of us. My mouth has never been spoiled, and I believe that was why the mistress preferred me to Ginger, although her paces were certainly quite as good. She used often to envy me, and said it was all the fault of breaking in, and the gag bit in London, that her mouth was not so perfect as mine; and then old Sir Oliver would say, “There, there! don't vex yourself; you have the greatest honor; a mare that can carry a tall man of our master's weight, with all your spring and sprightly action, does not need to hold her head down because she does not carry the lady; we horses must take things as they come, and always be contented and willing so long as we are kindly used.”
title: Black Beauty
author: Anna Sewell

Additionally, the rider expressed his gratitude to the governor before continuing on his journey. Shortly thereafter, we navigated one of the side streets and, upon reaching the midpoint of that street, turned into a particularly narrow thoroughfare characterized by rather modest residences on one side and what appeared to be coach houses and stables on the opposite side.

output:
“Thank you, governor,” and he rode on. We soon turned up one of the side streets, and about halfway up that we turned into a very narrow street, with rather poor-looking houses on one side, and what seemed to be coach-houses and stables on the other.

My owner pulled up at one of the houses and whistled. The door flew open, and a young woman, followed by a little girl and boy, ran out. There was a very lively greeting as my rider dismounted.
title: Black Beauty
author: Anna Sewell

input: Two days following the accident, Blantyre came to see me. He patted me and offered extensive praise. He informed Lord George that he believed the horse was aware of Annie's peril, just as he was. He stated, “I could not have controlled him even if I had wanted to; she should never ride another horse.” Through their discussion, I learned that my young mistress was now safe and would soon be able to ride again. This news brought me joy, and I began to anticipate a happy future.
output: Two days after the accident Blantyre paid me a visit; he patted me and praised me very much; he told Lord George that he was sure the horse knew of Annie's danger as well as he did. “I could not have held him in if I would,” said he, “she ought never to ride any other horse.” I found by their conversation that my young mistress was now out of danger, and would soon be able to ride again. This was good news to me and I looked forward to a happy life.
title: Black Beauty
author: Anna Sewell

It is worth noting that this is all very well; however, I must pose another question. Do you have no reason to suspect that, when he goes out with the horses to exercise them or to deliver a message, he may stop to converse with his acquaintances, or enter houses where he has no business, leaving the horses outside?

No, sir, certainly not; and if anyone has been saying such things about James, I do not believe it, and I do not intend to believe it unless it is fairly proved before witnesses. output:
“That's well; but I must put another question. Have you no reason to suspect, when he goes out with the horses to exercise them or to take a message, that he stops about talking to his acquaintances, or goes into houses where he has no business, leaving the horses outside?”

“No, sir, certainly not; and if anybody has been saying that about James, I don't believe it, and I don't mean to believe it unless I have it fairly proved before witnesses; it's not for me to say who has been trying to take away James' character, but I will say this, sir, that a steadier, pleasanter, honester, smarter young fellow I never had in this stable. I can trust his word and I can trust his work; he is gentle and clever with the horses, and I would rather have them in charge with him than with half the young fellows I know of in laced hats and liveries; and whoever wants a character of James Howard,” said John, with a decided jerk of his head, “let them come to John Manly.”
title: Black Beauty
author: Anna Sewell

input: Lady Harriet, who stayed at the hall, was often unwell and did not go out in the carriage. Lady Anne, on the other hand, tended to enjoy horseback riding with her brother or cousins. She was quite skilled at riding and was known to be cheerful and gentle, in addition to her beauty. She chose me as her horse and affectionately named me "Black Auster." I found these rides to be quite enjoyable, especially in the crisp, fresh air, sometimes accompanied by Ginger and at other times by Lizzie. Lizzie was a lively bay mare, almost thoroughbred, and was quite popular among the gentlemen due to her graceful movements and spirited nature. However, Ginger, who was more familiar with Lizzie, suggested that she could be somewhat anxious. Overall, these experiences tended to create a pleasant atmosphere for our rides.
output: The Lady Harriet, who remained at the hall, was a great invalid, and never went out in the carriage, and the Lady Anne preferred riding on horseback with her brother or cousins. She was a perfect horsewoman, and as gay and gentle as she was beautiful. She chose me for her horse, and named me “Black Auster”. I enjoyed these rides very much in the clear cold air, sometimes with Ginger, sometimes with Lizzie. This Lizzie was a bright bay mare, almost thoroughbred, and a great favorite with the gentlemen, on account of her fine action and lively spirit; but Ginger, who knew more of her than I did, told me she was rather nervous.
title: Black Beauty
author: Anna Sewell

input: Jerry maintained an exceptionally clean environment for us and provided as much variety in our diet as he could, ensuring that we received an ample quantity of food. Furthermore, he consistently supplied us with an adequate amount of clean, fresh water, which he allowed to remain accessible to us both day and night, with the exception of moments when we returned from our labor in a warm state. It is worth noting that some individuals believe that a horse should not have unrestricted access to water; however, I have observed that when we are permitted to drink according to our needs, we tend to consume only small amounts at a time. This approach benefits us significantly more than consuming large quantities all at once, which typically occurs when we are deprived of water until we become thirsty and uncomfortable. Additionally, some grooms would return home to enjoy their beer, leaving us with nothing but dry hay and oats for hours, without any moisture to accompany them. Consequently, we would inevitably consume excessive amounts of water in a single instance, which could negatively affect our respiratory health and sometimes lead to stomach discomfort. In essence, one of the most valuable aspects of our time here was the respite we received on Sundays. We exerted considerable effort throughout the week, and I sincerely believe that we would have struggled to maintain our stamina without that day of rest. Moreover, it provided us with the opportunity to enjoy each other's company, during which time I learned about the history of my companion.
output: Jerry kept us very clean, and gave us as much change of food as he could, and always plenty of it; and not only that, but he always gave us plenty of clean fresh water, which he allowed to stand by us both night and day, except of course when we came in warm. Some people say that a horse ought not to drink all he likes; but I know if we are allowed to drink when we want it we drink only a little at a time, and it does us a great deal more good than swallowing down half a bucketful at a time, because we have been left without till we are thirsty and miserable. Some grooms will go home to their beer and leave us for hours with our dry hay and oats and nothing to moisten them; then of course we gulp down too much at once, which helps to spoil our breathing and sometimes chills our stomachs. But the best thing we had here was our Sundays for rest; we worked so hard in the week that I do not think we could have kept up to it but for that day; besides, we had then time to enjoy each other's company. It was on these days that I learned my companion's history.
title: Black Beauty
author: Anna Sewell

input: She had not spoken to Edward in many years; their conversations were limited to logistical matters such as train schedules and hiring staff. That afternoon, however, she felt compelled to confront him. He was precisely as she remembered. It was akin to reopening a book after ten years, only to find the text unchanged. His motives remained the same. He had refrained from discussing the case because he did not want her to tarnish her thoughts with the notion that a brother officer could engage in blackmail. He sought to protect the reputation of his former love. However, it was clear that she was not concerned for her husband. He insisted repeatedly that there was nothing else in the world that could be held against him. She did not believe his assurances.
output: She had had no conversation with Edward for many years - none that went beyond the mere arrangements for taking trains or engaging servants. But that afternoon she had to let him have it. And he had been just the same as ever. It was like opening a book after a decade to find the words the same. He had the same motives. He had not wished to tell her about the case because he had not wished her to sully her mind with the idea that there was such a thing as a brother officer who could be a blackmailer - and he had wanted to protect the credit of his old light of love. That lady was certainly not concerned with her husband. And he swore, and swore, and swore, that there was nothing else in the world against him. She did not believe him.
title: The Good Soldier
author: Ford Madox Ford

input: This represents the saddest narrative I have ever encountered. My wife and I had been acquainted with the Ashburnhams for nine seasons in the town of Nauheim, cultivating a connection that was both intimate and characterized by a relaxed familiarity, akin to the relationship between a well-fitted glove and one’s hand. We were familiar with Captain and Mrs. Ashburnham to the extent that one could be acquainted with another individual; however, in a deeper sense, we were unaware of their true selves. It is worth noting that such a situation appears to be uniquely characteristic of English individuals. Until today, when I take the time to contemplate my understanding of this tragic situation, I must acknowledge that I knew virtually nothing about them. Moreover, six months prior, I had never visited England, and I certainly had not delved into the complexities of the English heart; my experiences had only skimmed the surface.
output: THIS is the saddest story I have ever heard. We had known the Ashburnhams for nine seasons of the town of Nauheim with an extreme intimacy - or, rather with an acquaintanceship as loose and easy and yet as close as a good glove's with your hand. My wife and I knew Captain and Mrs Ashburnham as well as it was possible to know anybody, and yet, in another sense, we knew nothing at all about them. This is, I believe, a state of things only possible with English people of whom, till today, when I sit down to puzzle out what I know of this sad affair, I knew nothing whatever. Six months ago I had never been to England, and, certainly, I had never sounded the depths of an English heart. I had known the shallows.
title: The Good Soldier
author: Ford Madox Ford

input: It was, after all, just under the mistletoe. Edward’s voice had a rather gruff quality to it. At that moment, Nancy entered, her footsteps quick as she climbed the stairs, quiet as she neared the open door of Leonora's room. Branshaw featured a spacious hall with wooden floors and animal skins. A gallery encircled this hall, providing access to Leonora's doorway. Even during her most intense headaches, she seemed to prefer having her door open, perhaps so she could hear the sound of approaching footsteps, which may have felt like impending trouble. In any case, she did not enjoy being in a room with a closed door. This preference for openness might suggest a desire for connection or awareness of her surroundings.
output: "Well, it was only under the mistletoe."... And there was Edward's gruff undertone. Then Nancy had come in, with feet that had hastened up the stairs and that tiptoed as they approached the open door of Leonora's room. Branshaw had a great big hall with oak floors and tiger skins. Round this hall there ran a gallery upon which Leonora's doorway gave. And even when she had the worst of her headaches she liked to have her door open - I suppose so that she might hear the approaching footsteps of ruin and disaster. At any rate she hated to be in a room with a shut door.
title: The Good Soldier
author: Ford Madox Ford

The group planned to embark on a retreat together and confess their sins, expressing their desire for this experience. 

Mr. Power remained silent, feeling outmaneuvered. However, a pleased expression briefly appeared on his face. 

Mr. Cunningham stated that all they needed to do was stand up with lighted candles in their hands and renew their baptismal vows. 

Mr. Kernan interjected, opposing the idea of using candles. He was aware of the impact he had made on his audience and continued to shake his head in disagreement. He also rejected the notion of the magic-lantern concept.
output:
“We’re all going to make a retreat together and confess our sins - and God knows we want it badly.”

Mr Power said nothing. He felt completely out-generalled. But a pleased expression flickered across his face.

“All we have to do,” said Mr Cunningham, “is to stand up with lighted candles in our hands and renew our baptismal vows.”

“I bar the candles,” said Mr Kernan, conscious of having created an effect on his audience and continuing to shake his head to and fro. “I bar the magic-lantern business.”
title: Dubliners
author: James Joyce

She wanted to remain on good terms with them, but even as she tried to be polite, her eyes kept following Mr Holohan as he moved along his limping, indirect route. They went down to a discreet part of the corridor. Mrs Kearney asked him when her daughter was going to be paid. Mr Holohan said that Mr Fitzpatrick was responsible for that. Mrs Kearney brought her daughter over to them, and talked to them amiably. She wanted to be on good terms with them but, while she strove to be polite, her eyes followed Mr Holohan in his limping and devious courses. As soon as she could she excused herself and went out after him.

input:
Mr. O’Connor had been hired by Tierney’s agent to campaign in one section of the ward. However, due to the unpleasant weather and his leaky boots, he spent much of the day by the fire in the Committee Room on Wicklow Street, accompanied by Jack, the elderly caretaker. They had been sitting there since darkness had fallen on the short October day. It was the sixth of October, and the outdoors was dreary and cold.

Mr. O’Connor tore a strip from the card and lit it to ignite his cigarette. As he did this, the flame illuminated a leaf of dark, glossy ivy tucked into the lapel of his coat. The old man observed him closely and then picked up the cardboard again, beginning to fan the fire gently while his companion smoked.
output:
Mr O’Connor had been engaged by Tierney’s agent to canvass one part of the ward but, as the weather was inclement and his boots let in the wet, he spent a great part of the day sitting by the fire in the Committee Room in Wicklow Street with Jack, the old caretaker. They had been sitting thus since the short day had grown dark. It was the sixth of October, dismal and cold out of doors.

Mr O’Connor tore a strip off the card and, lighting it, lit his cigarette. As he did so the flame lit up a leaf of dark glossy ivy in the lapel of his coat. The old man watched him attentively and then, taking up the piece of cardboard again, began to fan the fire slowly while his companion smoked.
title: Dubliners
author: James Joyce

input:
Delirium eventually subsides. He repeated her words, directing them inward: “What am I to do?” The instinct of the celibate urged him to restrain himself. However, the weight of his actions remained; even his sense of honor recognized that he needed to atone for this wrongdoing. 

As he sat beside her on the edge of the bed, Mary appeared at the door, informing him that the missus requested his presence in the parlour. He rose to don his coat and waistcoat, feeling more powerless than ever. Once he was dressed, he approached her to offer comfort. Everything would be fine, he assured her. He left her weeping on the bed, softly lamenting, “O my God!”
output:
But delirium passes. He echoed her phrase, applying it to himself: “What am I to do?” The instinct of the celibate warned him to hold back. But the sin was there; even his sense of honour told him that reparation must be made for such a sin.

While he was sitting with her on the side of the bed Mary came to the door and said that the missus wanted to see him in the parlour. He stood up to put on his coat and waistcoat, more helpless than ever. When he was dressed he went over to her to comfort her. It would be all right, never fear. He left her crying on the bed and moaning softly: “O my God!”
title: Dubliners
author: James Joyce

input: From this we may infer that when we believe any statement to be true, not because of the thing itself or because of principles of natural reason, but because of the authority and good opinion we have of the person who said it, then the speaker, or the person we believe in and trust, and whose word we accept, is the object of our faith, and the honor done in believing is done to that person alone. Consequently, when we believe that the Scriptures are the word of God, without having any immediate revelation from God himself, our belief, faith, and trust is in the Church, whose word we accept and rest upon. And those who believe what a prophet relates to them in the name of God accept the word of the prophet, do honor to him, and trust and believe in him regarding the truth of what he relates, whether he is a true prophet or a false one. And so it is also with all other history. For if I should not believe all that is written by historians about the glorious acts of Alexander or Caesar, I do not think the ghost of Alexander or Caesar would have any just cause to be offended, or anyone else except the historian. If Livy says the gods once made a cow speak, and we do not believe it, we do not distrust God in that, but Livy. So it is evident that whatever we believe on no other reason than what is drawn from the authority of men alone and their writings, whether they are sent from God or not, is faith in men only.
output: From whence we may inferre, that when wee believe any saying whatsoever it be, to be true, from arguments taken, not from the thing it selfe, or from the principles of naturall Reason, but from the Authority, and good opinion wee have, of him that hath sayd it; then is the speaker, or person we believe in, or trust in, and whose word we take, the object of our Faith; and the Honour done in Believing, is done to him onely. And consequently, when wee Believe that the Scriptures are the word of God, having no immediate revelation from God himselfe, our Beleefe, Faith, and Trust is in the Church; whose word we take, and acquiesce therein. And they that believe that which a Prophet relates unto them in the name of God, take the word of the Prophet, do honour to him, and in him trust, and believe, touching the truth of what he relateth, whether he be a true, or a false Prophet. And so it is also with all other History. For if I should not believe all that is written By Historians, of the glorious acts of Alexander, or Caesar; I do not think the Ghost of Alexander, or Caesar, had any just cause to be offended; or any body else, but the Historian. If Livy say the Gods made once a Cow speak, and we believe it not; wee distrust not God therein, but Livy. So that it is evident, that whatsoever we believe, upon no other reason, than what is drawn from authority of men onely, and their writings; whether they be sent from God or not, is Faith in men onely.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: This highlights that even when individuals are willing to adhere to laws, disputes regarding a person's actions can still arise. These disputes can be categorized into two main questions: first, whether an action was taken or not; and second, if an action was taken, whether it was in accordance with the law or not. The first type is referred to as a question of fact, while the second is identified as a question of right. Consequently, unless the parties involved agree to accept the decision of a third party, known as an arbitrator, they remain in a state of conflict. Ultimately, it is a principle of natural law that those in dispute should submit their rights to the judgment of an arbitrator.
output: And because, though men be never so willing to observe these Lawes, there may neverthelesse arise questions concerning a mans action; First, whether it were done, or not done; Secondly (if done) whether against the Law, or not against the Law; the former whereof, is called a question Of Fact; the later a question Of Right; therefore unlesse the parties to the question, Covenant mutually to stand to the sentence of another, they are as farre from Peace as ever. This other, to whose Sentence they submit, is called an ARBITRATOR. And therefore it is of the Law of Nature, "That they that are at controversie, submit their Right to the judgement of an Arbitrator."
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: When they are considered as his own, he is then called a natural person; and when they are considered as representing the words and actions of another, he is then a feigned or artificial person. It is worth noting that the word person is Latin; instead of it the Greeks have prosopon, which signifies the face, as persona in Latin signifies the disguise or outward appearance of a man, counterfeited on the stage, and sometimes more particularly that part of it which disguises the face, as a mask or visor. Furthermore, from the stage it has been transferred to any representer of speech and action, as well in tribunals as in theaters. In essence, a person is the same as an actor, both on the stage and in common conversation; and to personate is to act or represent oneself or another; and he who acts another is said to bear his person or act in his name (in which sense Cicero uses it when he says, "Unus Sustineo Tres Personas; Mei, Adversarii, & Judicis, I bear three persons: my own, my adversary's, and the judge's"), and is called on diverse occasions diversely, as a representer or representative, a lieutenant, a vicar, an attorney, a deputy, a procurator, an actor, and the like.
output:
When they are considered as his owne, then is he called a Naturall Person: And when they are considered as representing the words and actions of an other, then is he a Feigned or Artificiall person.

The word Person is latine: instead whereof the Greeks have Prosopon, which signifies the Face, as Persona in latine signifies the Disguise, or Outward Appearance of a man, counterfeited on the Stage; and somtimes more particularly that part of it, which disguiseth the face, as a Mask or Visard: And from the Stage, hath been translated to any Representer of speech and action, as well in Tribunalls, as Theaters. So that a Person, is the same that an Actor is, both on the Stage and in common Conversation; and to Personate, is to Act, or Represent himselfe, or an other; and he that acteth another, is said to beare his Person, or act in his name; (in which sence Cicero useth it where he saies, "Unus Sustineo Tres Personas; Mei, Adversarii, & Judicis, I beare three Persons; my own, my Adversaries, and the Judges;") and is called in diverse occasions, diversly; as a Representer, or Representative, a Lieutenant, a Vicar, an Attorney, a Deputy, a Procurator, an Actor, and the like.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: When the representative is a single individual, if he borrows money or incurs a debt through a contract, he alone bears responsibility; the other members do not share this liability. If the entity of the political body is embodied in one person who borrows money from an outsider—specifically, an individual who is not part of the same body—then the debt is solely that of the representative. This is because, should he possess authority through formal documentation to compel the members to repay what he has borrowed, he would consequently hold sovereignty over them. Therefore, such a grant would be void, as it stems from an error typically associated with human nature, and is an insufficient indication of the grantor's intent. Conversely, if the authority is acknowledged, the representative becomes sovereign, thereby falling outside the current discussion, which pertains solely to subordinate bodies. Consequently, no member is obligated to repay the borrowed debt; the responsibility rests solely with the representative. The lender, being an outsider to the formal documentation and the qualifications of the body, recognizes only those individuals who are engaged as debtors. Since the representative is capable of binding himself alone, he is the only debtor in this instance, and he must therefore repay the lender either from the common fund, if available, or from his own personal assets.
output: When The Representative Is One Man, If He Borrow Mony, Or Owe It, By Contract; He Is Lyable Onely, The Members Not If the person of the Body Politique being in one man, borrow mony of a stranger, that is, of one that is not of the same Body, (for no Letters need limit borrowing, seeing it is left to mens own inclinations to limit lending) the debt is the Representatives. For if he should have Authority from his Letters, to make the members pay what he borroweth, he should have by consequence the Soveraignty of them; and therefore the grant were either voyd, as proceeding from Errour, commonly incident to humane Nature, and an unsufficient signe of the will of the Granter; or if it be avowed by him, then is the Representer Soveraign, and falleth not under the present question, which is onely of Bodies subordinate. No member therefore is obliged to pay the debt so borrowed, but the Representative himselfe: because he that lendeth it, being a stranger to the Letters, and to the qualification of the Body, understandeth those onely for his debtors, that are engaged; and seeing the Representer can ingage himselfe, and none else, has him onely for Debtor; who must therefore pay him, out of the common stock (if there be any), or (if there be none) out of his own estate.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: If a guinea is the weekly pension of an individual, that person can use it to purchase a specific amount of necessities, comforts, and entertainment throughout the week. The extent of these purchases reflects the individual's actual wealth and their true weekly income. This income does not equate to both the guinea and the items it can buy; rather, it aligns more closely with one of these values. It is more accurate to consider the value of the goods purchased rather than the mere presence of the guinea itself.
output: Thus, if a guinea be the weekly pension of a particular person, he can in the course of the week purchase with it a certain quantity of subsistence, conveniencies, and amusements. In proportion as this quantity is great or small, so are his real riches, his real weekly revenue. His weekly revenue is certainly not equal both to the guinea and to what can be purchased with it, but only to one or other of those two equal values, and to the latter more properly than to the former, to the guinea’s worth rather than to the guinea.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: It is worth noting that there exist two scenarios in which it is generally beneficial to impose certain burdens on foreign goods to promote domestic industry. Additionally, there are two further situations in which it may warrant careful consideration: the first pertains to the extent to which it is appropriate to maintain the unrestricted importation of specific foreign goods, while the second concerns the degree and manner in which it may be suitable to reinstate such unrestricted importation after it has been temporarily suspended.
output: As there are two cases in which it will generally be advantageous to lay some burden upon foreign for the encouragement of domestic industry, so there are two others in which it may sometimes be a matter of deliberation, in the one, how far it is proper to continue the free importation of certain foreign goods; and, in the other, how far, or in what manner, it may be proper to restore that free importation, after it has been for some time interrupted.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
North America, while not as wealthy as England, is experiencing significant growth and advancing more rapidly towards greater wealth. A key indicator of a country's prosperity is its population growth. In Great Britain and many European nations, populations are not expected to double in less than five hundred years. In contrast, populations in the British colonies in North America have been observed to double in about twenty to twenty-five years. This increase in population is not primarily due to continuous immigration but rather to a high birth rate. It is reported that those who live into old age often see several dozen descendants. 

In North America, the rewards for labor are substantial, turning large families into sources of wealth rather than burdens for parents. Each child's labor is estimated to provide a significant financial benefit before they leave home. Additionally, a young widow with several children may be viewed positively in terms of potential marriage prospects, which is not the case in Europe where such women have limited opportunities. The value placed on children serves as a strong incentive for marriage, leading to a trend of early marriages among the population. Despite the rapid population growth resulting from these early unions, there remains a persistent complaint regarding the shortage of available labor. The demand for workers and the resources allocated for their support appear to be increasing more quickly than the supply of laborers.
output: But though North America is not yet so rich as England, it is much more thriving, and advancing with much greater rapidity to the further acquisition of riches. The most decisive mark of the prosperity of any country is the increase of the number of its inhabitants. In Great Britain, and most other European countries, they are not supposed to double in less than five hundred years. In the British colonies in North America, it has been found that they double in twenty or five-and-twenty years. Nor in the present times is this increase principally owing to the continual importation of new inhabitants, but to the great multiplication of the species. Those who live to old age, it is said, frequently see there from fifty to a hundred, and sometimes many more, descendants from their own body. Labour is there so well rewarded, that a numerous family of children, instead of being a burden, is a source of opulence and prosperity to the parents. The labour of each child, before it can leave their house, is computed to be worth a hundred pounds clear gain to them. A young widow with four or five young children, who, among the middling or inferior ranks of people in Europe, would have so little chance for a second husband, is there frequently courted as a sort of fortune. The value of children is the greatest of all encouragements to marriage. We cannot, therefore, wonder that the people in North America should generally marry very young. Notwithstanding the great increase occasioned by such early marriages, there is a continual complaint of the scarcity of hands in North America. The demand for labourers, the funds destined for maintaining them increase, it seems, still faster than they can find labourers to employ.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The price of the coarse metals, and still more that of the precious metals, at the most fertile mines in the world must necessarily more or less affect their price at every other mine. The price of copper in Japan must have some influence on its price at the copper mines in Europe. The price of silver in Peru, or the quantity of labour or of other goods it will purchase there, must have some influence on its price not only at the silver mines of Europe but also at those of China. After the discovery of the mines of Peru, most of the silver mines of Europe were abandoned. The value of silver was so much reduced that their produce could no longer pay the expense of working them or replace, with a profit, the food, clothes, lodging, and other necessaries consumed in that operation. This was also the case with the mines of Cuba and St. Domingo, and even with the ancient mines of Peru after the discovery of those of Potosi. Since the price of every metal at every mine is thus regulated in some measure by its price at the most fertile mine in the world that is actually worked, at most mines it can do little more than pay the expense of working and can seldom afford a very high rent to the landlord. This suggests that rent at most mines makes up but a small share of the price of the coarse metals and a still smaller share of that of the precious metals. Ultimately, labour and profit make up the greater part of both.
output: The price, therefore, of the coarse, and still more that of the precious metals, at the most fertile mines in the world, must necessarily more or less affect their price at every other in it. The price of copper in Japan must have some influence upon its price at the copper mines in Europe. The price of silver in Peru, or the quantity either of labour or of other goods which it will purchase there, must have some influence on its price, not only at the silver mines of Europe, but at those of China. After the discovery of the mines of Peru, the silver mines of Europe were, the greater part of them, abandoned. The value of silver was so much reduced, that their produce could no longer pay the expense of working them, or replace, with a profit, the food, clothes, lodging, and other necessaries which were consumed in that operation. This was the case, too, with the mines of Cuba and St. Domingo, and even with the ancient mines of Peru, after the discovery of those of Potosi. The price of every metal, at every mine, therefore, being regulated in some measure by its price at the most fertile mine in the world that is actually wrought, it can, at the greater part of mines, do very little more than pay the expense of working, and can seldom afford a very high rent to the landlord. Rent accordingly, seems at the greater part of mines to have but a small share in the price of the coarse, and a still smaller in that of the precious metals. Labour and profit make up the greater part of both.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The group proceeded to the back of the house, where they encountered a kitchen window. The Professor retrieved a small surgical saw from his case and handed it to a companion, indicating the iron bars protecting the window. The bars were cut through quickly, and using a long, thin knife, they managed to push back the sash fastening and open the window. The Professor entered first, followed by his companion. They observed that the kitchen and nearby servants' quarters were unoccupied. As they explored further, they discovered four servant-women lying on the dining-room floor, illuminated only by faint light filtering through the shutters. Their heavy breathing and the strong smell of laudanum indicated they were in a compromised state. The Professor and his companion exchanged glances, and he noted that they would address the women later. They then ascended to Lucy’s room. Briefly pausing at the door to listen for any sounds, they heard nothing and with anxious expressions, they gently opened the door and entered the room.
output: We went round to the back of the house, where there was a kitchen window. The Professor took a small surgical saw from his case, and handing it to me, pointed to the iron bars which guarded the window. I attacked them at once and had very soon cut through three of them. Then with a long, thin knife we pushed back the fastening of the sashes and opened the window. I helped the Professor in, and followed him. There was no one in the kitchen or in the servants’ rooms, which were close at hand. We tried all the rooms as we went along, and in the dining-room, dimly lit by rays of light through the shutters, found four servant-women lying on the floor. There was no need to think them dead, for their stertorous breathing and the acrid smell of laudanum in the room left no doubt as to their condition. Van Helsing and I looked at each other, and as we moved away he said: “We can attend to them later.” Then we ascended to Lucy’s room. For an instant or two we paused at the door to listen, but there was no sound that we could hear. With white faces and trembling hands, we opened the door gently, and entered the room.
title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker

After some time, I left him. The attendant informs me that he remained quiet until just before dawn, when he began to grow uneasy and eventually became violent. This continued until he fell into a paroxysm that exhausted him to the point of fainting into a sort of coma.

For three nights, the same pattern has occurred: violent throughout the day, then quiet from moonrise to sunrise. I wish I could find some clue as to the cause. It would almost seem as though some influence comes and goes. A fortunate idea has occurred to me. Tonight we shall pit sane minds against mad ones. He escaped before without our assistance; tonight he shall escape with it. We shall give him an opportunity, and have the men ready to follow in case they are needed.
output:
