input: A sound stirred me awake, perhaps the distant, sorrowful howling of dogs coming from far below in the valley, which I could not see. The sound seemed to resonate in my ears, and the dust particles around me appeared to shift shapes in response to it as they moved in the moonlight. I felt a struggle within me, as if my instincts—or perhaps my very essence—were trying to respond to this call. It was as though I were becoming entranced. The dust danced more rapidly, and the moonlight appeared to tremble as it passed through the surrounding darkness. Gradually, these lights formed vague, ghostly figures. Suddenly, I felt fully alert and bolted from the area, crying out in fear. The shapes that emerged from the moonlight were those of three spectral women, a haunting presence that I was destined to encounter. I sought refuge in my room, where the brightness of the lamp provided a sense of comfort, free from the moon’s eerie glow.
output: Something made me start up, a low, piteous howling of dogs somewhere far below in the valley, which was hidden from my sight. Louder it seemed to ring in my ears, and the floating motes of dust to take new shapes to the sound as they danced in the moonlight. I felt myself struggling to awake to some call of my instincts; nay, my very soul was struggling, and my half-remembered sensibilities were striving to answer the call. I was becoming hypnotised! Quicker and quicker danced the dust; the moonbeams seemed to quiver as they went by me into the mass of gloom beyond. More and more they gathered till they seemed to take dim phantom shapes. And then I started, broad awake and in full possession of my senses, and ran screaming from the place. The phantom shapes, which were becoming gradually materialised from the moonbeams, were those of the three ghostly women to whom I was doomed. I fled, and felt somewhat safer in my own room, where there was no moonlight and where the lamp was burning brightly.
title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker

input: I took his hand and made him a promise. I held the door open as he walked away, watching him enter his room and close the door behind him. As I stood there without moving, I noticed one of the maids quietly pass by in the hallway—she had her back to me and did not see me—before entering the room where Lucy was. This moment touched me. Devotion can often be uncommon, and we tend to feel a deep sense of gratitude towards those who show it willingly to the ones we care about. Here was a young woman putting aside her understandable fears of death to keep vigil by the side of her beloved mistress, ensuring that the poor body would not be alone until it was finally laid to rest. This act reflects the depth of human connection and kindness.
output: I took his hand, and promised him. I held my door open as he went away, and watched him go into his room and close the door. As I stood without moving, I saw one of the maids pass silently along the passage - she had her back towards me, so did not see me - and go into the room where Lucy lay. The sight touched me. Devotion is so rare, and we are so grateful to those who show it unasked to those we love. Here was a poor girl putting aside the terrors which she naturally had of death to go watch alone by the bier of the mistress whom she loved, so that the poor clay might not be lonely till laid to eternal rest....
title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker

input: On May 18, the individual revisited the room during daylight to seek clarity about the situation. Upon reaching the doorway at the top of the stairs, they discovered that the door was closed and had been forcefully pushed against the frame, resulting in splintered woodwork. It was noted that the lock bolt had not been engaged, indicating that the door was secured from the inside. This suggests that the previous experience was not merely a dream, prompting the individual to consider taking action based on this assumption.
output: 18 May. - I have been down to look at that room again in daylight, for I must know the truth. When I got to the doorway at the top of the stairs I found it closed. It had been so forcibly driven against the jamb that part of the woodwork was splintered. I could see that the bolt of the lock had not been shot, but the door is fastened from the inside. I fear it was no dream, and must act on this surmise.
title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker

input: The concentration of all significant talent within the governing body can ultimately hinder its mental activity and capacity for progress. As a collective entity, the officials operate within a system that relies heavily on established rules, which can lead to complacency and habitual routines. When they do deviate from this routine, it often results in unexamined ideas influenced by prominent individuals within the group. The only effective way to counterbalance these opposing tendencies—complacency and impulsive ideas—is through the scrutiny of equally capable individuals outside the governing body. This highlights the necessity for independent avenues to cultivate talent and provide the experiences needed for sound judgment in practical matters. To ensure a proficient and innovative group of officials, it is crucial that not all tasks that nurture the skills needed for governance are monopolized by the governing body. This approach helps prevent the decline of the bureaucracy into a mere adherence to outdated practices.
output: It is not, also, to be forgotten, that the absorption of all the principal ability of the country into the governing body is fatal, sooner or later, to the mental activity and progressiveness of the body itself. Banded together as they are - working a system which, like all systems, necessarily proceeds in a great measure by fixed rules - the official body are under the constant temptation of sinking into indolent routine, or, if they now and then desert that mill-horse round, of rushing into some half-examined crudity which has struck the fancy of some leading member of the corps: and the sole check to these closely allied, though seemingly opposite, tendencies, the only stimulus which can keep the ability of the body itself up to a high standard, is liability to the watchful criticism of equal ability outside the body. It is indispensable, therefore, that the means should exist, independently of the government, of forming such ability, and furnishing it with the opportunities and experience necessary for a correct judgment of great practical affairs. If we would possess permanently a skilful and efficient body of functionaries - above all, a body able to originate and willing to adopt improvements; if we would not have our bureaucracy degenerate into a pedantocracy, this body must not engross all the occupations which form and cultivate the faculties required for the government of mankind.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: I have saved for the last a large class of questions about the limits of government interference. These questions are closely connected with the subject of this Essay, but strictly speaking they do not belong to it. In these cases, the reasons against interference do not rest on the principle of liberty. The question is not about restraining the actions of individuals but about helping them. It is asked whether the government should do something for their benefit, or cause it to be done, instead of leaving it to be done by the individuals themselves, either singly or in voluntary combination.
output: I have reserved for the last place a large class of questions respecting the limits of government interference, which, though closely connected with the subject of this Essay, do not, in strictness, belong to it. These are cases in which the reasons against interference do not turn upon the principle of liberty: the question is not about restraining the actions of individuals, but about helping them: it is asked whether the government should do, or cause to be done, something for their benefit, instead of leaving it to be done by themselves, individually, or in voluntary combination.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input:
There exists a realm of action where society, as a collective, tends to have only an indirect interest, which includes aspects of a person's life and behavior that primarily impact themselves. While it is possible that these aspects may also affect others, this occurs only with their free and informed consent and participation. When referring to affecting oneself, it is important to note that this is in a direct and initial sense; what influences an individual may subsequently influence others through that individual. This potential for broader impact will be addressed later. Thus, this area represents the appropriate domain of personal liberty. 

It encompasses, first, the inner realm of consciousness, which calls for freedom of conscience in a broad sense. This includes the freedom to think and feel, as well as complete freedom of opinion and sentiment on all matters, whether practical, speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The freedom to express and share opinions might appear to be governed by a different principle, since it pertains to an individual’s actions that involve others. However, it is often almost as significant as the freedom of thought itself and is largely based on similar reasoning, making it practically inseparable from it. Second, this principle advocates for the liberty of personal tastes and pursuits, allowing individuals to design their lives according to their own characters and to act as they wish, provided that their actions do not harm others, regardless of whether those others may perceive their choices as unwise or misguided. Third, from this individual liberty arises the freedom to form associations among individuals, enabling them to unite for any purpose that does not cause harm to others, assuming that those involved are of legal age and are not coerced or misled. In summary, the domain of human liberty encompasses individual thought, expression, personal pursuits, and the freedom to associate, all under the condition that these do not harm others.
output: But there is a sphere of action in which society, as distinguished from the individual, has, if any, only an indirect interest; comprehending all that portion of a person's life and conduct which affects only himself, or if it also affects others, only with their free, voluntary, and undeceived consent and participation. When I say only himself, I mean directly, and in the first instance: for whatever affects himself, may affect others through himself; and the objection which may be grounded on this contingency, will receive consideration in the sequel. This, then, is the appropriate region of human liberty. It comprises, first, the inward domain of consciousness; demanding liberty of conscience, in the most comprehensive sense; liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects, practical or speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The liberty of expressing and publishing opinions may seem to fall under a different principle, since it belongs to that part of the conduct of an individual which concerns other people; but, being almost of as much importance as the liberty of thought itself, and resting in great part on the same reasons, is practically inseparable from it. Secondly, the principle requires liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like, subject to such consequences as may follow: without impediment from our fellow-creatures, so long as what we do does not harm them, even though they should think our conduct foolish, perverse, or wrong. Thirdly, from this liberty of each individual, follows the liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite, for any purpose not involving harm to others: the persons combining being supposed to be of full age, and not forced or deceived.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It is worth noting that there exist numerous acts which, while they may only cause direct harm to the individuals who engage in them, should not be subject to legal prohibition. However, when such acts are performed in public, they constitute a breach of social decorum and, consequently, may be legitimately restricted under the category of offenses against others. Offenses against decency exemplify this concept; further elaboration on these matters is unnecessary, particularly since they are only tangentially related to our primary topic. The objection to public display is equally applicable to many actions that are not inherently reprehensible or perceived as such.
output: Again, there are many acts which, being directly injurious only to the agents themselves, ought not to be legally interdicted, but which, if done publicly, are a violation of good manners and coming thus within the category of offences against others may rightfully be prohibited. Of this kind are offences against decency; on which it is unnecessary to dwell, the rather as they are only connected indirectly with our subject, the objection to publicity being equally strong in the case of many actions not in themselves condemnable, nor supposed to be so.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

output:
“You must follow me carefully. I shall have to controvert one or two ideas that are almost universally accepted. The geometry, for instance, they taught you at school is founded on a misconception.”

“Is not that rather a large thing to expect us to begin upon?” said Filby, an argumentative person with red hair.

“I do not mean to ask you to accept anything without reasonable ground for it. You will soon admit as much as I need from you. You know of course that a mathematical line, a line of thickness nil, has no real existence. They taught you that? Neither has a mathematical plane. These things are mere abstractions.”
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: Doubts began to arise for me. I wondered why the Morlocks might have taken my Time Machine, as I felt fairly certain they were responsible. It also made me curious why, if the Eloi were in charge, they could not retrieve the machine for me. Additionally, I found myself questioning their overwhelming fear of the dark. I attempted to discuss these matters with Weena, but I was somewhat let down by her responses. Initially, she appeared not to understand my questions, and eventually, she seemed unwilling to engage with the topic. She shivered, indicating that it might be too distressing for her. When I pressed her for more information, perhaps a bit too insistently, she began to cry. Those were the only tears I witnessed during that Golden Age, apart from my own. Seeing her distress shifted my focus completely; I became more concerned with alleviating her sadness than with the Morlocks. Before long, she was smiling and clapping her hands while I carefully burned a match. Ultimately, this moment highlighted the complexities of our emotions in that time.
output: “Then came troublesome doubts. Why had the Morlocks taken my Time Machine? For I felt sure it was they who had taken it. Why, too, if the Eloi were masters, could they not restore the machine to me? And why were they so terribly afraid of the dark? I proceeded, as I have said, to question Weena about this Underworld, but here again I was disappointed. At first she would not understand my questions, and presently she refused to answer them. She shivered as though the topic was unendurable. And when I pressed her, perhaps a little harshly, she burst into tears. They were the only tears, except my own, I ever saw in that Golden Age. When I saw them I ceased abruptly to trouble about the Morlocks, and was only concerned in banishing these signs of her human inheritance from Weena’s eyes. And very soon she was smiling and clapping her hands, while I solemnly burnt a match.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: I travel to London and observe the bustling crowds on Fleet Street and the Strand. It occurs to me that they are merely the phantoms of the past, haunting the thoroughfares that I have witnessed as silent and forlorn. These figures move back and forth, mere specters in a lifeless city, embodying a mockery of existence within a reanimated form. Furthermore, it is a peculiar experience to stand on Primrose Hill, as I did just one day prior to composing this final chapter. I behold the vast expanse of houses, appearing dim and blue through the haze of smoke and mist, gradually disappearing into the indistinct lower sky. I observe people strolling amidst the flower beds on the hill and sightseers gathered around the Martian machine that remains stationary. I hear the joyous noise of children at play and reflect on the time when I perceived all these sights as bright and distinct, sharp and silent, beneath the dawn of that last significant day.
output: I go to London and see the busy multitudes in Fleet Street and the Strand, and it comes across my mind that they are but the ghosts of the past, haunting the streets that I have seen silent and wretched, going to and fro, phantasms in a dead city, the mockery of life in a galvanised body. And strange, too, it is to stand on Primrose Hill, as I did but a day before writing this last chapter, to see the great province of houses, dim and blue through the haze of the smoke and mist, vanishing at last into the vague lower sky, to see the people walking to and fro among the flower beds on the hill, to see the sight-seers about the Martian machine that stands there still, to hear the tumult of playing children, and to recall the time when I saw it all bright and clear-cut, hard and silent, under the dawn of that last great day....
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: At around six in the evening, I sat with my wife in the summerhouse, discussing the imminent battle with fervor. Suddenly, I heard a muffled explosion coming from the common, followed swiftly by a barrage of gunfire. Soon after, a violent crash reverberated nearby, shaking the ground beneath us. As I stepped onto the lawn, I witnessed the treetops near the Oriental College erupt in a smoky red flame, while the tower of the adjacent church collapsed into ruins. The pinnacle of the mosque had completely disappeared, and the roofline of the college appeared as though it had been struck by a heavy artillery shell. One of our chimneys cracked with a sound resembling a gunshot, then broke apart, sending debris tumbling onto the tiles and creating a pile of shattered red fragments on the flower bed beside my study window.
output: About six in the evening, as I sat at tea with my wife in the summerhouse talking vigorously about the battle that was lowering upon us, I heard a muffled detonation from the common, and immediately after a gust of firing. Close on the heels of that came a violent rattling crash, quite close to us, that shook the ground; and, starting out upon the lawn, I saw the tops of the trees about the Oriental College burst into smoky red flame, and the tower of the little church beside it slide down into ruin. The pinnacle of the mosque had vanished, and the roof line of the college itself looked as if a hundred-ton gun had been at work upon it. One of our chimneys cracked as if a shot had hit it, flew, and a piece of it came clattering down the tiles and made a heap of broken red fragments upon the flower bed by my study window.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
The artilleryman shared his observations about the types of individuals who still remained in London. 

"Not long ago," he mentioned, "some individuals managed to restore the electric lights, resulting in Regent Street and the Circus being brightly lit and filled with intoxicated individuals, both men and women, who appeared to be celebrating and making noise until dawn. This was recounted to me by someone who witnessed it. As daylight approached, they noticed a fighting-machine nearby the Langham, observing them. It’s unclear how long it had been there, but it likely startled some of the people present. The machine then moved down the street and collected nearly a hundred individuals who were either too inebriated or frightened to escape." 

In summary, the artilleryman painted a picture of a chaotic scene marked by both celebration and fear in the city.
output:
The artilleryman began to tell me of the sort of people who still remained in London.

“One night last week,” he said, “some fools got the electric light in order, and there was all Regent Street and the Circus ablaze, crowded with painted and ragged drunkards, men and women, dancing and shouting till dawn. A man who was there told me. And as the day came they became aware of a fighting-machine standing near by the Langham and looking down at them. Heaven knows how long he had been there. It must have given some of them a nasty turn. He came down the road towards them, and picked up nearly a hundred too drunk or frightened to run away.”
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
She was moving swiftly, appearing within moments to be positioned midway between the steamboat and the Martians, a dark silhouette against the vast, flat stretch of the Essex coast. 

Suddenly, the leading Martian lowered his tube and released a canister of black gas toward the ironclad. The canister struck her left side and deflected off, creating a dark plume that rolled out to sea, a flowing mass of black smoke from which the ironclad swiftly escaped. To the observers on the steamboat, sitting low in the water with the sun glaring in their eyes, it appeared as if she was already in the midst of the Martians.
output:
She was steaming at such a pace that in a minute she seemed halfway between the steamboat and the Martians - a diminishing black bulk against the receding horizontal expanse of the Essex coast.

Suddenly the foremost Martian lowered his tube and discharged a canister of the black gas at the ironclad. It hit her larboard side and glanced off in an inky jet that rolled away to seaward, an unfolding torrent of Black Smoke, from which the ironclad drove clear. To the watchers from the steamer, low in the water and with the sun in their eyes, it seemed as though she were already among the Martians.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: Unable to discern the situation from his window, my brother decided to step outside into the street just as the sky began to brighten with dawn's early light. The number of people rushing by, both on foot and in vehicles, seemed to increase with each passing moment. He heard shouts of “Black Smoke!” echoing through the crowd, and the repetition of such a widespread fear was likely to be contagious. As my brother stood uncertainly on the doorstep, he noticed another newsvendor approaching and quickly purchased a paper. The vendor was hurrying away with the others, selling his papers for a shilling each as he ran, reflecting a strange mixture of urgency and commerce. In summary, the scene captured the chaotic atmosphere of the moment, blending fear and the instinct to profit.
output: Unable from his window to learn what was happening, my brother went down and out into the street, just as the sky between the parapets of the houses grew pink with the early dawn. The flying people on foot and in vehicles grew more numerous every moment. “Black Smoke!” he heard people crying, and again “Black Smoke!” The contagion of such a unanimous fear was inevitable. As my brother hesitated on the door-step, he saw another newsvendor approaching, and got a paper forthwith. The man was running away with the rest, and selling his papers for a shilling each as he ran - a grotesque mingling of profit and panic.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
By eight o’clock, a number of boys and unemployed men had already commenced their journey to the common in order to observe the “dead men from Mars.” This was the form that the story took. I first became aware of it from my newspaper boy at approximately a quarter to nine when I ventured out to retrieve my Daily Chronicle. I was understandably startled and did not delay in making my way across the Ottershaw bridge to the sand-pits.

Upon my arrival, I discovered a small crowd of approximately twenty individuals gathered around the substantial hole in which the cylinder rested. I have previously described the appearance of that colossal object, embedded in the earth. The turf and gravel surrounding it appeared charred, as if subjected to a sudden explosion. It is likely that its impact had generated a flash of fire. Henderson and Ogilvy were not present. I believe they realized that there was nothing that could be accomplished at that moment and had departed to have breakfast at Henderson’s residence.
output:
By eight o’clock a number of boys and unemployed men had already started for the common to see the “dead men from Mars.” That was the form the story took. I heard of it first from my newspaper boy about a quarter to nine when I went out to get my Daily Chronicle. I was naturally startled, and lost no time in going out and across the Ottershaw bridge to the sand-pits.

I found a little crowd of perhaps twenty people surrounding the huge hole in which the cylinder lay. I have already described the appearance of that colossal bulk, embedded in the ground. The turf and gravel about it seemed charred as if by a sudden explosion. No doubt its impact had caused a flash of fire. Henderson and Ogilvy were not there. I think they perceived that nothing was to be done for the present, and had gone away to breakfast at Henderson’s house.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: Atalanta is not the first or the last maiden whom greed for gold has led to defile the temple of Love. Moreover, it is not only maidens but also men who, in the race of life, sink from the high and generous ideals of youth to the gambler's code of the stock exchange. In all our nation's striving, is the Gospel of Work not corrupted by the Gospel of Pay? This is so common that one half of people consider it normal. It is so unquestioned that we almost fear to ask whether the end of racing is gold and whether the proper aim of man is to be rich. If this is the fault of America, how dire a danger lies before a new land and a new city, lest Atlanta, stooping for mere gold, shall find that gold accursed.
output: Atalanta is not the first or the last maiden whom greed of gold has led to defile the temple of Love; and not maids alone, but men in the race of life, sink from the high and generous ideals of youth to the gambler’s code of the Bourse; and in all our Nation’s striving is not the Gospel of Work befouled by the Gospel of Pay? So common is this that one-half think it normal; so unquestioned, that we almost fear to question if the end of racing is not gold, if the aim of man is not rightly to be rich. And if this is the fault of America, how dire a danger lies before a new land and a new city, lest Atlanta, stooping for mere gold, shall find that gold accursed!

input: I have so far attempted to clarify the physical, economic, and political relations between Negroes and whites in the South as I have understood them, including crime and education for the reasons already given. Yet beyond these more tangible matters of human contact, there remains an essential part of any proper description of the South that is difficult to describe or define in terms easily understood by outsiders. It is, in short, the atmosphere of the land, the thought and feeling, and the countless small actions that together constitute daily life. In any community or nation, these small things are the most elusive to grasp and yet the most essential to a clear understanding of group life as a whole. What is true of all communities is especially true of the South, where, beyond written history and printed law, there has been unfolding for a generation a profound storm and stress of human souls, an intense ferment of feeling, and an intricate writhing of spirit such as few peoples have experienced. Within and beyond the somber veil of color, vast social forces have been at work: efforts for human betterment, movements toward disintegration and despair, tragedies and comedies in social and economic life, and a shifting and rising and falling of human hearts that have made this land one of mingled sorrow and joy, of change and excitement and unrest.
output: I have thus far sought to make clear the physical, economic, and political relations of the Negroes and whites in the South, as I have conceived them, including, for the reasons set forth, crime and education. But after all that has been said on these more tangible matters of human contact, there still remains a part essential to a proper description of the South which it is difficult to describe or fix in terms easily understood by strangers. It is, in fine, the atmosphere of the land, the thought and feeling, the thousand and one little actions which go to make up life. In any community or nation it is these little things which are most elusive to the grasp and yet most essential to any clear conception of the group life taken as a whole. What is thus true of all communities is peculiarly true of the South, where, outside of written history and outside of printed law, there has been going on for a generation as deep a storm and stress of human souls, as intense a ferment of feeling, as intricate a writhing of spirit, as ever a people experienced. Within and without the sombre veil of color vast social forces have been at work, - efforts for human betterment, movements toward disintegration and despair, tragedies and comedies in social and economic life, and a swaying and lifting and sinking of human hearts which have made this land a land of mingled sorrow and joy, of change and excitement and unrest.

input: The discovery of the golden fleece signifies a notable development; it has not only been located but is also being produced in its region of origin. The operation of cotton mills represents a significant aspect of the modern economy in the New South. Throughout the Carolinas and Georgia, extending into Mexico, one can observe the presence of these large, utilitarian structures, which, despite their simple appearance, are characterized by a bustling and noisy activity that contrasts with the surrounding landscape. This suggests that the Cotton Kingdom continues to play an important role, as its influence persists. Furthermore, markets that once resisted newcomers have gradually expanded overseas and have begun to move toward the Black Belt region, indicating a shift in economic dynamics.
output: And now the golden fleece is found; not only found, but, in its birthplace, woven. For the hum of the cotton-mills is the newest and most significant thing in the New South to-day. All through the Carolinas and Georgia, away down to Mexico, rise these gaunt red buildings, bare and homely, and yet so busy and noisy withal that they scarce seem to belong to the slow and sleepy land. Perhaps they sprang from dragons’ teeth. So the Cotton Kingdom still lives; the world still bows beneath her sceptre. Even the markets that once defied the parvenu have crept one by one across the seas, and then slowly and reluctantly, but surely, have started toward the Black Belt.

He caught up the next paper; it was a brief note in the doctor’s hand and dated at the top. “O Poole!” the lawyer cried, “he was alive and here this day. input: The besiegers, perhaps unsettled by the chaos they had just caused and the sudden silence that followed, instinctively stepped back and looked inside. Before them, in the gentle light of the lamp, was a cabinet, with a warm fire flickering and crackling in the hearth, the kettle softly whistling a delicate tune. A few drawers were ajar, and papers were neatly arranged on the business table, while closer to the fire, items were prepared for tea. It was likely the quietest room one might imagine, and, aside from the glass-fronted cabinets filled with chemicals, it could be described as one of the most ordinary spaces that night in London. Overall, it presented a striking contrast to the turmoil outside.
output: The besiegers, appalled by their own riot and the stillness that had succeeded, stood back a little and peered in. There lay the cabinet before their eyes in the quiet lamplight, a good fire glowing and chattering on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin strain, a drawer or two open, papers neatly set forth on the business table, and nearer the fire, the things laid out for tea; the quietest room, you would have said, and, but for the glazed presses full of chemicals, the most commonplace that night in London.
title: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

input: Men have historically engaged others to carry out their illicit activities while maintaining their own safety and reputation. This highlights a unique phenomenon in which I was the first to employ this practice for personal enjoyment. I was able to navigate public life with an air of respectability, and, in an instant, shed that façade to embrace a sense of freedom. Ultimately, I found complete security in my concealed existence. This suggests a profound detachment; I did not even have to take direct responsibility for my actions. By simply retreating to my laboratory, allowing myself a brief moment to prepare and consume a concoction that I always kept at hand, I could make Edward Hyde disappear as easily as a breath vanishes from a mirror. In his place, I would quietly return home, tending to my studies with a sense of assurance that allowed me to dismiss any doubts about my character.
output: Men have before hired bravos to transact their crimes, while their own person and reputation sat under shelter. I was the first that ever did so for his pleasures. I was the first that could plod in the public eye with a load of genial respectability, and in a moment, like a schoolboy, strip off these lendings and spring headlong into the sea of liberty. But for me, in my impenetrable mantle, the safety was complete. Think of it - I did not even exist! Let me but escape into my laboratory door, give me but a second or two to mix and swallow the draught that I had always standing ready; and whatever he had done, Edward Hyde would pass away like the stain of breath upon a mirror; and there in his stead, quietly at home, trimming the midnight lamp in his study, a man who could afford to laugh at suspicion, would be Henry Jekyll.
title: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

output:

input: A careful observer might have noticed that the subject was unpleasant; however, the doctor addressed it cheerfully. "My poor Utterson," he remarked, "you are unfortunate to have such a client. I have never seen a man as troubled as you were by my will, except perhaps that rigid scholar, Lanyon, who disapproves of what he calls my scientific theories. I recognize that he is a good man—you need not frown—an excellent individual, and I always intend to spend more time with him. Nevertheless, he is still a rigid scholar, an uninformed and loud scholar. I have never been more let down by any man than I have been by Lanyon."
output: A close observer might have gathered that the topic was distasteful; but the doctor carried it off gaily. “My poor Utterson,” said he, “you are unfortunate in such a client. I never saw a man so distressed as you were by my will; unless it were that hide-bound pedant, Lanyon, at what he called my scientific heresies. O, I know he’s a good fellow - you needn’t frown - an excellent fellow, and I always mean to see more of him; but a hide-bound pedant for all that; an ignorant, blatant pedant. I was never more disappointed in any man than Lanyon.”

input: October was a beautiful month at Green Gables. The birches in the hollow turned as golden as sunshine, the maples behind the orchard were royal crimson, and the wild cherry trees along the lane took on the loveliest shades of dark red and bronzy green, while the fields rested in their aftermath. One Saturday morning, Anne came dancing in with her arms full of gorgeous boughs. “Oh, Marilla,” she exclaimed, “I’m so glad I live in a world where there are Octobers. It would be terrible if we just skipped from September to November, wouldn’t it? Look at these maple branches. Don’t they give you a thrill—several thrills? I’m going to decorate my room with them.” This highlights how deeply Anne responds to the changing seasons, and her delight suggests a lively appreciation for the beauty around her. Ultimately, the passage conveys a simple, wholehearted joy in the month of October.
output:
OCTOBER was a beautiful month at Green Gables, when the birches in the hollow turned as golden as sunshine and the maples behind the orchard were royal crimson and the wild cherry-trees along the lane put on the loveliest shades of dark red and bronzy green, while the fields sunned themselves in aftermaths.

“Oh, Marilla,” she exclaimed one Saturday morning, coming dancing in with her arms full of gorgeous boughs, “I’m so glad I live in a world where there are Octobers. input: The situation was somewhat more challenging on the platform of the large concert hall at the hotel, where she soon found herself. The bright electric lights may have overwhelmed her senses, and the combination of perfumes and background chatter tended to confuse her. She found herself wishing she could be seated in the audience alongside Diana and Jane, who appeared to be enjoying themselves quite well at the back. Instead, she was squeezed between a robust lady in pink silk and a tall girl in a white lace dress who looked somewhat disdainful. The stout lady occasionally turned her head to scrutinize Anne through her glasses, making Anne feel increasingly uncomfortable and, at times, as if she might cry out. Meanwhile, the girl in white lace was speaking quite loudly to her neighbor, making comments about the "country bumpkins" and "rustic belles" in attendance, seemingly looking forward to the entertainment of local talent. Anne couldn’t help but feel a strong dislike for the white-lace girl. In summary, the entire experience was proving to be more than a little overwhelming for her.
output: It was still worse on the platform of the big concert hall of the hotel, where she presently found herself. The electric lights dazzled her eyes, the perfume and hum bewildered her. She wished she were sitting down in the audience with Diana and Jane, who seemed to be having a splendid time away at the back. She was wedged in between a stout lady in pink silk and a tall, scornful-looking girl in a white-lace dress. The stout lady occasionally turned her head squarely around and surveyed Anne through her eyeglasses until Anne, acutely sensitive of being so scrutinized, felt that she must scream aloud; and the white-lace girl kept talking audibly to her next neighbor about the “country bumpkins” and “rustic belles” in the audience, languidly anticipating “such fun” from the displays of local talent on the program. Anne believed that she would hate that white-lace girl to the end of life.
title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L. M. Montgomery

input: Anne expressed her determination to engage with young girls respectfully, emphasizing that she would not laugh at their use of complex vocabulary, as she recognized the emotional impact this could have. She then recounted an experience with Diana, where they attempted to make taffy for the first time. Unfortunately, the taffy did not turn out well because neither of them had prior experience. During the process, Diana left Anne to stir while she prepared the plates, leading to the taffy burning. Additionally, a cat walked across one plate, resulting in its disposal. Despite these setbacks, Anne found the activity to be enjoyable. Upon returning home, Mrs. Barry invited Anne to visit frequently, while Diana affectionately waved goodbye from the window. This highlights Anne's sense of joy and connection, as she noted feeling inspired to create a new prayer to commemorate the day's events.
output: “Well, anyway, when I am grown up,” said Anne decidedly, “I’m always going to talk to little girls as if they were too, and I’ll never laugh when they use big words. I know from sorrowful experience how that hurts one’s feelings. After tea Diana and I made taffy. The taffy wasn’t very good, I suppose because neither Diana nor I had ever made any before. Diana left me to stir it while she buttered the plates and I forgot and let it burn; and then when we set it out on the platform to cool the cat walked over one plate and that had to be thrown away. But the making of it was splendid fun. Then when I came home Mrs. Barry asked me to come over as often as I could and Diana stood at the window and threw kisses to me all the way down to Lover’s Lane. I assure you, Marilla, that I feel like praying tonight and I’m going to think out a special brand-new prayer in honor of the occasion.”
title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L. M. Montgomery

“You may want to reflect on your lessons and assignments,” Marilla suggested, hiding her pleasure at how the situation was unfolding. “If you’re returning to school, I hope we won’t have to hear about slates being broken over people’s heads and similar antics. It would be best to behave yourself and follow your teacher’s instructions.” 

“I’ll do my best to be a good student,” Anne replied with a hint of sadness. “I don’t think it will be very enjoyable. Mr. Phillips mentioned that Minnie Andrews is a model student, but she seems to lack imagination and excitement. She appears rather dull and doesn’t seem to have much fun. However, I’m feeling so down that it might actually be easier for me now. I’ll take the longer route instead. I really wouldn’t want to walk the Birch Path all by myself; it would be too upsetting.” 

In summary, both characters express their thoughts about school while reflecting on the need for good behavior and the emotional challenges that come with it.
output:
“You’d better muse over your lessons and sums,” said Marilla, concealing her delight at this development of the situation. “If you’re going back to school I hope we’ll hear no more of breaking slates over people’s heads and such carryings on. Behave yourself and do just what your teacher tells you.”

“I’ll try to be a model pupil,” agreed Anne dolefully. “There won’t be much fun in it, I expect. Mr. Phillips said Minnie Andrews was a model pupil and there isn’t a spark of imagination or life in her. She is just dull and poky and never seems to have a good time. But I feel so depressed that perhaps it will come easy to me now. I’m going round by the road. I couldn’t bear to go by the Birch Path all alone. I should weep bitter tears if I did.”
title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L. M. Montgomery

input:
After Anne left, Marilla attended to her evening chores, feeling quite unsettled. She was deeply concerned about her valuable brooch. What if Anne had misplaced it? It was infuriating that the girl denied taking it when it was clear to anyone that she must have. Her innocent face only added to Marilla’s frustration.

“I cannot think of anything worse,” Marilla reflected as she nervously shelled peas. “I do not believe she intended to steal it. She probably took it to play with or to fuel her imagination. It is obvious she must have taken it, as no one else had been in that room since she left, according to her own account, until I went up tonight. The brooch is undoubtedly missing. I assume she has lost it and is too frightened to admit it for fear of punishment. It is upsetting to consider that she tells lies. This is a far more serious issue than her earlier temper. It is a heavy burden to care for a child whom one cannot trust. Deception and dishonesty are what she has shown. I must admit I feel worse about that than about the brooch itself. If she had only told the truth, I would not feel as troubled.”
output:
When Anne had gone Marilla went about her evening tasks in a very disturbed state of mind. She was worried about her valuable brooch. What if Anne had lost it? And how wicked of the child to deny having taken it, when anybody could see she must have! With such an innocent face, too!

“I don’t know what I wouldn’t sooner have had happen,” thought Marilla, as she nervously shelled the peas. “Of course, I don’t suppose she meant to steal it or anything like that. She’s just taken it to play with or help along that imagination of hers. She must have taken it, that’s clear, for there hasn’t been a soul in that room since she was in it, by her own story, until I went up tonight. And the brooch is gone, there’s nothing surer. I suppose she has lost it and is afraid to own up for fear she’ll be punished. It’s a dreadful thing to think she tells falsehoods. It’s a far worse thing than her fit of temper. It’s a fearful responsibility to have a child in your house you can’t trust. Slyness and untruthfulness - that’s what she has displayed. I declare I feel worse about that than about the brooch. If she’d only have told the truth about it I wouldn’t mind so much.”
title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L. M. Montgomery

input:
Marilla remained silent about the incident with Matthew that evening. However, when Anne continued to be difficult the following morning, an explanation was necessary to clarify her absence from the breakfast table. Marilla explained the entire situation to Matthew, making a conscious effort to convey the seriousness of Anne's actions.

"Rachel Lynde deserved a reprimand; she is a meddlesome old gossip," Matthew replied in a soothing manner.

"Matthew Cuthbert, I am shocked by your response. You recognize that Anne's actions were unacceptable, yet you defend her. I suppose you will argue next that she should not face any consequences at all."
output:
MARILLA said nothing to Matthew about the affair that evening; but when Anne proved still refractory the next morning an explanation had to be made to account for her absence from the breakfast table. Marilla told Matthew the whole story, taking pains to impress him with a due sense of the enormity of Anne’s behavior.

“It’s a good thing Rachel Lynde got a calling down; she’s a meddlesome old gossip,” was Matthew’s consolatory rejoinder.

“Matthew Cuthbert, I’m astonished at you. You know that Anne’s behavior was dreadful, and yet you take her part! I suppose you’ll be saying next thing that she oughtn’t to be punished at all!”
title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L. M. Montgomery

input: Diana expressed her feelings by saying, “You might miss out on a lot of fun. We may be building a charming new house near the brook, and we’ll likely be playing ball next week, which you have not tried before, Anne. It can often be quite exciting. Additionally, we are planning to learn a new song, which Jane Andrews is currently practicing, and Alice Andrews is expected to bring a new Pansy book next week. We could all read it aloud, taking turns by the brook. And you know how much you enjoy reading aloud, Anne.”  In summary, Diana highlighted the enjoyable activities that may take place and encouraged Anne to consider joining in.
output: “Just think of all the fun you will miss,” mourned Diana. “We are going to build the loveliest new house down by the brook; and we’ll be playing ball next week and you’ve never played ball, Anne. It’s tremendously exciting. And we’re going to learn a new song - Jane Andrews is practicing it up now; and Alice Andrews is going to bring a new Pansy book next week and we’re all going to read it out loud, chapter about, down by the brook. And you know you are so fond of reading out loud, Anne.”
title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L. M. Montgomery

Despite her intense dislike for Gilbert, she loved Diana deeply, with the full force of her passionate heart, equally strong in its preferences and aversions. One evening, Marilla returned from the orchard carrying a basket of apples and discovered Anne sitting by the east window in the fading light, crying uncontrollably.

"It is about Diana," Anne sobbed dramatically. "I love Diana so much, Marilla. I cannot imagine living without her. However, I know that as we grow older, Diana will marry and leave me. What will I do then? I detest her husband; I truly despise him. I have envisioned the entire event—the wedding and everything. Diana will be dressed in white, adorned with a veil, looking as beautiful and regal as a queen, while I will stand as the bridesmaid in a lovely dress with puffed sleeves, concealing a broken heart beneath my smiling exterior. Then I will have to say goodbye to Diana…" At this point, Anne completely broke down and wept with escalating sorrow.
output:
As much as she hated Gilbert, however, did she love Diana, with all the love of her passionate little heart, equally intense in its likes and dislikes. One evening Marilla, coming in from the orchard with a basket of apples, found Anne sitting along by the east window in the twilight, crying bitterly.

“It’s about Diana,” sobbed Anne luxuriously. “I love Diana so, Marilla. I cannot ever live without her. But I know very well when we grow up that Diana will get married and go away and leave me. And oh, what shall I do? I hate her husband - I just hate him furiously. I’ve been imagining it all out - the wedding and everything - Diana dressed in snowy garments, with a veil, and looking as beautiful and regal as a queen; and me the bridesmaid, with a lovely dress too, and puffed sleeves, but with a breaking heart hid beneath my smiling face. And then bidding Diana goodbye-e-e - ” Here Anne broke down entirely and wept with increasing bitterness.
title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L. M. Montgomery

output:

input: It is worth noting that the reason it is natural to refer to this principle as a law of thought lies in the fact that we rely on thought, rather than external observation, to convince ourselves of its necessary truth. After we have observed that a tree is a beech, we do not need to examine it again to confirm that it is not also a beech; our reasoning alone informs us that such a contradiction is impossible. However, the conclusion that the law of contradiction is solely a law of thought is, in fact, erroneous. When we accept the law of contradiction, we do not assert that the mind is constructed in such a way that it must adhere to this law. Rather, this acceptance emerges as a subsequent outcome of psychological reflection, which itself presupposes an initial belief in the law of contradiction. The belief in this law pertains to the nature of reality and not merely to the realm of thought. It is not, for example, the conviction that if we consider a specific tree to be a beech, we cannot simultaneously consider it to be not a beech; instead, it is the assertion that if the tree is a beech, it cannot concurrently be not a beech. Consequently, the law of contradiction pertains to the nature of things rather than merely to thoughts; while the belief in the law of contradiction qualifies as a thought, the law itself constitutes a fact regarding the entities in the world. If the assertion we make when we accept the law of contradiction were not true concerning the nature of reality, the necessity of our belief would not render the law of contradiction true; this indicates that the law cannot be classified solely as a law of thought.
output: Now what makes it natural to call this principle a law of thought is that it is by thought rather than by outward observation that we persuade ourselves of its necessary truth. When we have seen that a tree is a beech, we do not need to look again in order to ascertain whether it is also not a beech; thought alone makes us know that this is impossible. But the conclusion that the law of contradiction is a law of thought is nevertheless erroneous. What we believe, when we believe the law of contradiction, is not that the mind is so made that it must believe the law of contradiction. This belief is a subsequent result of psychological reflection, which presupposes the belief in the law of contradiction. The belief in the law of contradiction is a belief about things, not only about thoughts. It is not, e.g., the belief that if we think a certain tree is a beech, we cannot at the same time think that it is not a beech; it is the belief that if the tree is a beech, it cannot at the same time be not a beech. Thus the law of contradiction is about things, and not merely about thoughts; and although belief in the law of contradiction is a thought, the law of contradiction itself is not a thought, but a fact concerning the things in the world. If this, which we believe when we believe the law of contradiction, were not true of the things in the world, the fact that we were compelled to think it true would not save the law of contradiction from being false; and this shows that the law is not a law of thought.

input: In derivative knowledge, it is essential that our ultimate premises possess a certain degree of self-evidence, as must the connection between these premises and the conclusions derived from them. For instance, consider a reasoning process in geometry. It is insufficient for the axioms upon which we base our reasoning to be self-evident; it is equally necessary that, at each stage of the reasoning, the relationship between premises and conclusions be self-evident as well. In complex reasoning, this connection often exhibits only a minimal degree of self-evidence; consequently, errors in reasoning are not unlikely when the difficulty of the task is considerable.
output: In derivative knowledge our ultimate premisses must have some degree of self-evidence, and so must their connexion with the conclusions deduced from them. Take for example a piece of reasoning in geometry. It is not enough that the axioms from which we start should be self-evident: it is necessary also that, at each step in the reasoning, the connexion of premiss and conclusion should be self-evident. In difficult reasoning, this connexion has often only a very small degree of self-evidence; hence errors of reasoning are not improbable where the difficulty is great.

It can often happen that some of our beliefs are mistaken, which leads us to consider how we might distinguish knowledge from error, if it is possible at all. This concern is not present in the context of knowledge by acquaintance, since, regardless of the specific object of acquaintance, even in cases like dreams and hallucinations, no error occurs as long as we focus on the immediate object. Error tends to arise only when we interpret the immediate object, or sense-datum, as indicative of some external physical object. Therefore, the challenges associated with knowledge of truths may be more complex than those linked to knowledge of objects. To begin addressing the issues related to knowledge of truths, let us first investigate the nature and scope of our intuitive judgments.
output: If the above account is correct, all our knowledge of truths depends upon our intuitive knowledge. It therefore becomes important to consider the nature and scope of intuitive knowledge, in much the same way as, at an earlier stage, we considered the nature and scope of knowledge by acquaintance. But knowledge of truths raises a further problem, which does not arise in regard to knowledge of things, namely the problem of error. Some of our beliefs turn out to be erroneous, and therefore it becomes necessary to consider how, if at all, we can distinguish knowledge from error. This problem does not arise with regard to knowledge by acquaintance, for, whatever may be the object of acquaintance, even in dreams and hallucinations, there is no error involved so long as we do not go beyond the immediate object: error can only arise when we regard the immediate object, i.e. the sense-datum, as the mark of some physical object. Thus the problems connected with knowledge of truths are more difficult than those connected with knowledge of things. Suddenly one of these gypsies, in trembling opal, seizes a cocktail out of the air, dumps it down for courage and, moving her hands like Frisco, dances out alone on the canvas platform. A momentary hush; the orchestra leader varies his rhythm obligingly for her, and there is a burst of chatter as the erroneous news goes around that she is Gilda Gray’s understudy from the Follies. The party has begun.

I believe that on the first night I went to Gatsby’s house I was one of the few guests who had actually been invited. People were not invited - they went there. They got into automobiles which bore them out to Long Island, and somehow they ended up at Gatsby’s door. Once there they were introduced by somebody who knew Gatsby, and after that they conducted themselves according to the rules of behaviour associated with an amusement park. Sometimes they came and went without having met Gatsby at all, came for the party with a simplicity of heart that was its own ticket of admission.
title: The Great Gatsby
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald

input: Rose expressed her emotions to the doctor, indicating that her aunt had given him full authority over the situation. She requested that he not be excessively harsh on the individuals involved. The doctor responded by suggesting that Rose seemed to believe that everyone, apart from herself, was inclined to be unkind on that day. He commented that he hoped for the sake of young men that she would be found in a similarly sympathetic state when approached by a young man seeking her compassion. He added that he wished he were younger so he could take advantage of the present opportunity to do so.
output:
“Then my aunt invests you with full power,” said Rose, smiling through her tears; “but pray don’t be harder upon the poor fellows than is indispensably necessary.”

“You seem to think,” retorted the doctor, “that everybody is disposed to be hard-hearted today, except yourself, Miss Rose. I only hope, for the sake of the rising male sex generally, that you may be found in as vulnerable and soft-hearted a mood by the first eligible young fellow who appeals to your compassion; and I wish I were a young fellow, that I might avail myself, on the spot, of such a favourable opportunity for doing so, as the present.”
title: Oliver Twist
author: Charles Dickens

input: A slight commotion in the courtroom drew his attention back to the proceedings. He observed that the jurors had gathered to deliberate their verdict. As he scanned the gallery, he noted people straining to see his face; some were quickly adjusting their glasses, while others whispered to their neighbors, their expressions reflecting strong disapproval. A small number seemed indifferent to him and focused solely on the jury, appearing impatient with the delay. Ultimately, he found no expression of sympathy directed toward him in any of the faces present, including those of the many women in attendance. Instead, the prevailing sentiment was a keen interest in the possibility of his condemnation.
output: A slight bustle in the court, recalled him to himself. Looking round, he saw that the jurymen had turned together, to consider their verdict. As his eyes wandered to the gallery, he could see the people rising above each other to see his face: some hastily applying their glasses to their eyes: and others whispering their neighbours with looks expressive of abhorrence. A few there were, who seemed unmindful of him, and looked only to the jury, in impatient wonder how they could delay. But in no one face - not even among the women, of whom there were many there - could he read the faintest sympathy with himself, or any feeling but one of all-absorbing interest that he should be condemned.
title: Oliver Twist
author: Charles Dickens

input:
He roamed across vast stretches of land yet always returned to the familiar place. Morning transitioned into noon, and the day began to fade. Despite this, he continued to wander back and forth, up and down, and around the same area. Eventually, he managed to leave and set his direction toward Hatfield. 

At nine o’clock in the evening, the man, exhausted, and the dog, limping from unusual exertion, descended the hill past the church of the peaceful village. They made their way along the narrow street and entered a small public house, its dim light guiding them to safety. A fire crackled in the tap-room, where several local laborers were gathered, enjoying their drinks.
output:
He wandered over miles and miles of ground, and still came back to the old place. Morning and noon had passed, and the day was on the wane, and still he rambled to and fro, and up and down, and round and round, and still lingered about the same spot. At last he got away, and shaped his course for Hatfield.

It was nine o’clock at night, when the man, quite tired out, and the dog, limping and lame from the unaccustomed exercise, turned down the hill by the church of the quiet village, and plodding along the little street, crept into a small public-house, whose scanty light had guided them to the spot. There was a fire in the tap-room, and some country-labourers were drinking before it.
title: Oliver Twist
author: Charles Dickens

The bluff appears uniform from the cave hollow, with no houses or wood-yards and bushes that look the same. However, do you notice that white area up there where a landslide occurred? That is one of my markers. We will get ashore now.

Huck examined the surrounding area but found nothing. Tom confidently entered a dense cluster of sumach bushes and stated, "Money. You make them raise as much as they can from their friends, and after keeping them for a year, if they have not raised anything, you kill them. That is the general method. However, you do not kill the women. You simply confine them, but you do not harm them. They are always beautiful, wealthy, and extremely frightened. You take their watches and belongings, but you always remove your hat and speak courteously. There are no individuals as polite as robbers, as you will find in any book. Eventually, the women start to develop feelings for you. After spending one or two weeks in the cave, they cease crying, and you could not persuade them to leave. If you attempted to drive them out, they would immediately return. This is a common theme in all the books."
output:
“Now you see this bluff here looks all alike all the way down from the cave hollow - no houses, no wood-yards, bushes all alike. But do you see that white place up yonder where there’s been a landslide? Well, that’s one of my marks. We’ll get ashore, now.”

Huck searched all the place about, and found nothing. Tom proudly marched into a thick clump of sumach bushes and said:

“Money. You make them raise all they can, off’n their friends; and after you’ve kept them a year, if it ain’t raised then you kill them. That’s the general way. Only you don’t kill the women. You shut up the women, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and awfully scared. You take their watches and things, but you always take your hat off and talk polite. They ain’t anybody as polite as robbers - you’ll see that in any book. Well, the women get to loving you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two weeks they stop crying and after that you couldn’t get them to leave. If you drove them out they’d turn right around and come back. It’s so in all the books.”
title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Complete

input: I proceeded along the bank with one eye watching for Pap and the other watching for whatever the rising water might bring. Suddenly a canoe appeared, a fine one about thirteen or fourteen feet long, riding high like a duck. I dove headfirst off the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and struck out for the canoe. I expected someone might be lying down in it, since people often did that to fool folks, and when a man had pulled a skiff almost to it they would raise up and laugh at him. That was not the case this time. It was a drift canoe for certain, and I climbed in and paddled it ashore. I thought the old man would be glad when he saw it, for it was worth ten dollars. When I reached shore, however, Pap was not yet in sight, and as I was running the canoe into a little creek like a gully, all hung over with vines and willows, another idea struck me. I decided I would hide it well, and then, instead of taking to the woods when I ran off, I would go about fifty miles down the river and camp in one place for good, avoiding such a rough time tramping on foot.
output: I went along up the bank with one eye out for pap and t’other one out for what the rise might fetch along. Well, all at once here comes a canoe; just a beauty, too, about thirteen or fourteen foot long, riding high like a duck. But when I got to shore pap wasn’t in sight yet, and as I was running her into a little creek like a gully, all hung over with vines and willows, I struck another idea: I judged I’d hide her good, and then, ’stead of taking to the woods when I run off, I’d go down the river about fifty mile and camp in one place for good, and not have such a rough time tramping on foot.

input: A month or two ago, when Peter first fell ill, he expressed a sense of resignation about his recovery. That letter was the only document Peter was willing to write.
output: “Oh, yes; a month or two ago, when Peter was first took; because Peter said then that he sorter felt like he warn’t going to get well this time. You see, he was pretty old, and George’s g’yirls was too young to be much company for him, except Mary Jane, the red-headed one; and so he was kinder lonesome after George and his wife died, and didn’t seem to care much to live. He most desperately wanted to see Harvey - and William, too, for that matter - because he was one of them kind that can’t bear to make a will. Laws knows that I may have wanted to visit Tom badly enough to consider going, and I had every intention to do so; however, after a certain point, I really wouldn’t have gone, even for great rewards. 

Yet, both she and Tom occupied my thoughts, leading to a rather restless night. I found myself wandering down the path twice during the night, quietly approaching the front. Each time, I noticed her sitting by the candle in the window, gazing down the road with tears in her eyes. I wished I could do something to help her, but I felt powerless, aside from promising myself that I would never again do anything to upset her. When I awoke at dawn for the third time and slipped back down, she was still there. Her candle was nearly extinguished, and her head was resting on her hand as she slept. In summary, my concern for her and my determination to avoid causing her distress were strong throughout the night.
output:
Laws knows I wanted to go bad enough to see about Tom, and was all intending to go; but after that I wouldn’t a went, not for kingdoms.

But she was on my mind and Tom was on my mind, so I slept very restless. And twice I went down the rod away in the night, and slipped around front, and see her setting there by her candle in the window with her eyes towards the road and the tears in them; and I wished I could do something for her, but I couldn’t, only to swear that I wouldn’t never do nothing to grieve her any more. And the third time I waked up at dawn, and slid down, and she was there yet, and her candle was most out, and her old gray head was resting on her hand, and she was asleep.
title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain

“Here and here,” replied Catherine, as she struck one hand against her forehead and the other against her breast. “In whichever place the soul resides, I am convinced in both my soul and my heart that I am in error.” 

She settled herself beside me once more; her expression became increasingly somber and serious, and her clasped hands began to tremble. 

“Oh, do not, Miss Catherine!” I exclaimed. “We are already dismal enough without summoning ghosts and visions to trouble us. Come, let us be joyful and true to yourself! Observe little Hareton; he is not dreaming of anything gloomy. How sweetly he smiles in his sleep!”
output:
“Here! and here!” replied Catherine, striking one hand on her forehead, and the other on her breast: “in whichever place the soul lives. In my soul and in my heart, I’m convinced I’m wrong!”

She seated herself by me again: her countenance grew sadder and graver, and her clasped hands trembled.

“Oh! don’t, Miss Catherine!” I cried. “We’re dismal enough without conjuring up ghosts and visions to perplex us. Come, come, be merry and like yourself! Look at little Hareton! he’s dreaming nothing dreary. How sweetly he smiles in his sleep!”

The old woman responded, “Regarding the gentleman you may have harmed, it seems that you might find it difficult ahead, perhaps even more so than you anticipate. However, that is not my concern; my role is to care for you and ensure you recover. I approach my duty with a clear conscience; it would be beneficial if everyone did the same.” 

I turned away, feeling a sense of discomfort towards someone who could express such a cold remark to someone who had just been saved from the brink of death. I felt weak and unable to process everything that had occurred. My entire life seemed to me like a dream; at times, I questioned whether it was all real, as it did not come to me with the clarity of true experience.
output:
“For that matter,” replied the old woman, “if you mean about the gentleman you murdered, I believe that it were better for you if you were dead, for I fancy it will go hard with you! However, that’s none of my business; I am sent to nurse you and get you well; I do my duty with a safe conscience; it were well if everybody did the same.”

I turned with loathing from the woman who could utter so unfeeling a speech to a person just saved, on the very edge of death; but I felt languid and unable to reflect on all that had passed. The whole series of my life appeared to me as a dream; I sometimes doubted if indeed it were all true, for it never presented itself to my mind with the force of reality.

output: The lion then composed himself on his back on a sofa on one side of the drinking-table, while the jackal sat at his own paper-bestrewn table proper, on the other side of it, with the bottles and glasses ready to his hand. Both resorted to the drinking-table without stint, but each in a different way; the lion for the most part reclining with his hands in his waistband, looking at the fire, or occasionally flirting with some lighter document; the jackal, with knitted brows and intent face, so deep in his task, that his eyes did not even follow the hand he stretched out for his glass - which often groped about, for a minute or more, before it found the glass for his lips. Two or three times, the matter in hand became so knotty, that the jackal found it imperative on him to get up, and steep his towels anew. From these pilgrimages to the jug and basin, he returned with such eccentricities of damp headgear as no words can describe; which were made the more ludicrous by his anxious gravity.

output:
He stared at her with a fearful look, and after a while his lips began to form some words, though no sound proceeded from them. By degrees, in the pauses of his quick and laboured breathing, he was heard to say:

With the tears streaming down her face, she put her two hands to her lips, and kissed them to him; then clasped them on her breast, as if she laid his ruined head there.

Not yet trusting the tones of her voice, she sat down on the bench beside him. He recoiled, but she laid her hand upon his arm. A strange thrill struck him when she did so, and visibly passed over his frame; he laid the knife down softly, as he sat staring at her.
